regions.name: The Heartlands
regions.tagline: Where a bell still rings at noon and the roads are mostly paved.
regions.history_long:
Before the Heartlands were the Heartlands, they were nothing — a river plain between two low ranges, grazed by aurochs and crossed by nomads who left no name. The first permanent settlement was a waystation called Aldren's Rest, built by a band of retired sellswords who decided they were too old to die useful deaths and too young to stop eating. Aldren himself is remembered in no song, but his well still stands, half-buried behind the Heartlands market square, and children sometimes drop copper coins down it on feast days.

The kingdom proper coalesced during what the scholars call the Granary Centuries — three hundred years when the harvests were freakishly, almost suspiciously generous, and the surplus drew craftsmen, priests, and opportunists the way a fresh loaf draws flies. By the time the weather returned to normal, the Heartlands had guilds, a crown, a mint, a tax code, and the conviction that it had always been this way. The conviction is the most durable of those achievements. Every other kingdom that has risen on Aelgard has looked at the Heartlands and thought: that is what permanence ought to feel like.

It was not, of course, permanent. The Spellfire War burned Old Aldren to the foundations and scattered the original noble houses so thoroughly that three of the current baronies are held by the descendants of kitchen staff. The crown rebuilt, because the crown always rebuilds, and the rebuilt city has the odd lopsided charm of a thing pieced together from memory. The bell tower at the centre of the market is the third to stand on that spot, and the bell itself is the second recast of a bell that melted when the wizards took the walls. Nobody mentions this. Every noon, the bell rings, and the carters pull their wagons aside, and everyone agrees, without saying so, that this is how a city is supposed to sound.

The Heartlands is not the oldest kingdom on Aelgard and it is not the strongest. What it is, is the most comfortable. The roads are paved — not all of them, and not well, but paved enough that a cart can reach the Veilwood border in three days without a broken axle. The guilds will train you if you can pay and gate you if you cannot, which is what guilds everywhere do, but at least here the rules are written down. The priests of the Last Light keep a flame burning in every chapel in every village, and when the flame goes out, a Lamplighter replaces it, and nobody asks too many questions about why this matters. It matters because it has always mattered.

If you arrive here as an outsider, the first thing you will notice is that the people are busy without being frantic. The second thing you will notice is that nobody watches the sky for what might be coming. They have forgotten how. They are not wrong to have forgotten — the Heartlands is genuinely, specifically safe, ringed by its guard patrols and its paved roads and its ordinary weather. But step out of it, in any direction, and the world remembers things the Heartlands has chosen not to.
regions.current_state:
The crown is currently held by a council of three regents, because the last queen died without naming an heir and the three most plausible claimants agreed, after an awkward week, that none of them actually wanted the job. The arrangement has held for eleven years, which is eleven years longer than anyone predicted. The regents argue in public and agree in private, and the city runs.

Tension lives in the guilds more than in the palace. The Smiths want more tin than the mines are producing. The Apothecaries say the Farming Guild is hoarding ranarr. The Lamplighters — a strange, old order that everyone forgets to count as a guild until a flame goes out — are quietly grieving: three of their senior members vanished in the last year, and nobody has returned from looking for them. Walk into the market and you will see all of this layered: the shout of the grain criers, the slow patrol of the guard, and the one Lamplighter on the corner, holding a candle that is always lit, watching the road north.
regions.geography:
A broad river plain bracketed by low grass hills, with a river — the Aldrin — running roughly east-west and meeting the sea far to the southwest. The soil is deep and tillable. Orchards climb the southern slopes. North of the city, the land rises into scrub that eventually becomes the Wilds. To the east, a paved road threads through hills toward the Sootworks; to the west, another reaches the Veilwood.

Climate is temperate. Summers are warm and long, winters short and damp. Storms come in from the southwest in spring.

factions.name: The Three Regents
factions.description: A council of three — a merchant, a general, and a priest — who rule the Heartlands by mutual reluctance since the last queen died heirless. They hold formal court once a month and informal court every night over wine.
factions.attitude_to_player: polite to anyone with manners, generous to anyone who completes a Heartlands quest, wary of adventurers who ask too many questions about the northern border

factions.name: The Lamplighters Guild
factions.description: An old religious order that tends the Last Light — a sacred flame kept burning in every Heartlands chapel. They claim the flame was lit from a coal taken from Aelgard's first hearth, and that if it ever goes out in every chapel at once, something specific and bad will happen. They will not say what.
factions.attitude_to_player: warm if you ever light a flame in a chapel, cold if you ever extinguish one, and they notice either way

factions.name: The Six Guilds
factions.description: Smiths, Fishers, Cooks, Miners, Warriors, and Magi — the backbone of Heartlands commerce and training. Entry is gated by skill and modest fees. The guildmasters feud politely and protect each other ferociously when outsiders criticize any of them.
factions.attitude_to_player: transactional at first, then quietly loyal once you've earned your medallion

factions.name: The Grain Criers
factions.description: The daily-price-shouters of the market square. Not officially a faction, but they know everything that moves in or out of the Heartlands, because they watch prices for a living.
factions.attitude_to_player: friendly if tipped, invaluable if courted

landmarks.name: The Chapel of the Last Light
landmarks.description: The oldest chapel in the city, one narrow stone nave with a flame that has not gone out since the city was rebuilt. The current priest is very old and has not left the chapel in thirty years.
landmarks.secret: Behind the altar stone, if you've completed The Culinaromancer's Curse and the priest has come to trust you, a loose slab lifts onto a narrow stair down. What is down there is not explained to anyone who has not been down before.

landmarks.name: The Grand Hall
landmarks.description: A teleport hub linking the six Heartlands guilds under one vaulted roof. Built into the hill behind the palace. Opens only after the Grand Feast has been survived.
landmarks.secret: The six guildmasters each have a private alcove here, and the alcoves are not the same size. The Cook's is largest. Nobody will explain why.

landmarks.name: The Old Mill
landmarks.description: A flour mill on the Aldrin, abandoned after the miller drowned in his own wheel. Ghost-touched grain still grows in the field behind it; the crop is richer, and the harvest smells faintly of river water.
landmarks.secret: The miller is not entirely gone. On certain nights, the wheel turns without wind or current, and the flour that comes out is whiter than anything a living mill can produce.

landmarks.name: The Noble Mansion Row
landmarks.description: A crescent of stone houses north of the palace where the remaining old-blood families live. The rows are patrolled but porous — a thief with nerve and a good route can make a fortune here in a single night.
landmarks.secret: One of the five houses is empty. It has been empty for four generations, and the family's name has been carefully removed from every record. The door opens only with a key that has never been found.

landmarks.name: The Aldrin Crossing
landmarks.description: The stone bridge at the centre of the city. Five arches, built in one piece after the Spellfire War. Traders gather at the north end every morning.
landmarks.secret: The fourth arch from the east, if you crouch under it at low water, shows a carved sigil that does not match the mason's marks on the others. The sigil is faint but it is not weathered.

regions.music_mood: a slow hammered string against a hearth-warm drone — familiar enough to feel like coming home, patient enough to suggest that home has been waiting
regions.weather: temperate and reliable, long summer evenings, damp autumn mornings, short winters that frost the orchards but rarely the roads
regions.colors: worn sandstone, wheat gold, slate blue river, dark oak timber, the cream-and-red of Heartlands banners; lanterns at dusk turn the whole city amber

regions.name: The Boneyard Wastes
regions.tagline: The sand is pale here because it was bleached, and it was bleached by something.
regions.history_long:
The Wastes were once a sea. Not a recent sea — a primordial one, deep enough for leviathans, still enough for their bones to settle in the silt without breaking. What happened to the water is the first question any traveller asks, and the answer is the Cataclysm, which is the answer to most questions about the Wastes, and which is less an answer than a shrug.

The Cataclysm is what the Hermit of the Old Sun calls it, because the Hermit is the only living person who claims to remember the world from before. Whether the Hermit is telling the truth depends on who you ask. The archaeologists say no: too long ago, no one could survive it. The nomads say possibly: the desert preserves strange things, and the Hermit's eyes are the wrong color for a man who has lived only one lifetime. The Hermit himself says little. He sits under a sun-bleached awning at the oasis and drinks water from a clay cup, and if you bring him a leviathan bone, he will tell you exactly one true thing in exchange, and not a second one.

Before the Cataclysm, the land beneath the sea was something called Kherem. The archaeologists have reconstructed that much from the buried pyramids. Kherem had pharaohs — that word is native, not borrowed — and the pharaohs built tombs the size of hills, and the tombs are still there, sunk into the sand like the vertebrae of the leviathans they share a bed with. Azhmari was one of the last pharaohs, and he did not intend to die the way he died, and he has not entirely finished dying. Most of what walks the Wastes at night walks because Azhmari has not finished.

The nomads came later, much later, from somewhere south that no longer exists. They brought the trade routes with them, strung across the dunes as a network of oasis-to-oasis crossings that the crown does not recognise and cannot police. The nomads do not need the crown to recognise them. They have water, and the crown does not. The oasis at the heart of the Wastes is the only reliable water for ninety miles in any direction, and the nomads control it, and they let the archaeologists work because the archaeologists pay in salt and in news from the Heartlands, both of which the nomads value.

The Wastes are salted. This is worth saying directly, because nothing the crown's scholars have written explains it well. The sand is not just dry — it is salt-scoured, as if every storm for ten thousand years has left another layer of brine that the sun then cooked off. Crops will not grow. Metal rusts in strange patterns. Water, where you find it, tastes faintly of the sea that was. And under the salt, the bones: leviathan spines long enough to sight a horizon down, scarab carapaces the size of shields, skulls that cannot plausibly belong to anything that ever lived on land. The archaeologists catalogue them slowly. The nomads walk around them. The skeletons, which also walk, do not walk around anything.
regions.current_state:
Razak's oasis camp is the only safe ground. The archaeologist Veris has set up her tent there because her excavation at the leviathan graveyard has turned up a buried pyramid and she cannot work at night anymore. The Hermit sits and will sit. The nomads are tense — three of their regular routes have been closed by sandstorms that are not seasonal and that seem to begin at Azhmari's buried throne. A prince who will not stay buried is not a political problem the nomads care to solve, but it is now their water problem, and water is the only thing they care to solve.

Azhmari himself has begun recruiting. This is new. The skeletons used to wander — now they gather, in loose formations, facing his pyramid. Nobody has asked them why. Nobody has been foolish enough to ask them anything.
regions.geography: Rolling dunes cut by ancient dry riverbeds. A single oasis at the centre, fed by a spring nobody can locate. Leviathan skeletons half-buried in the sand like landmarks. Buried pyramids, their capstones sometimes protruding after a strong wind. To the north the dunes thin into the Heartlands borderlands; to the east the swamp of Moryskah begins abruptly where the salt gives way to black water.

factions.name: Razak's Nomads
factions.description: Traders and water-keepers who have held the oasis for longer than any crown has held its throne. They trade in salt, embalming materials, and information, and they speak a language that is older than any written record, though they all also speak traders' common.
factions.attitude_to_player: neutral and watchful; warm if you respect the water, cold permanently if you waste it

factions.name: The Excavation Society
factions.description: A loose group of scholars, led by Archaeologist Veris, who catalogue what the sand gives up. They are not wealthy, not connected, and not protected, but they are persistent. They have mapped eleven pyramids and believe there are forty-three.
factions.attitude_to_player: grateful for any help, generous with shared findings, dangerously prone to asking you to go deeper than you meant to

factions.name: The Hermit's Silent Order
factions.description: Possibly one man. Possibly more. The Hermit does not claim followers but there are four other awnings at the oasis where people sit in silence for long hours, and the nomads treat them as a group.
factions.attitude_to_player: answers one true question per bone you bring; tells you nothing otherwise

factions.name: The Remnant of Kherem
factions.description: Azhmari's risen dead, gathered in loose formations near his buried throne. Not a faction in any political sense, but a presence that behaves as though it has a plan.
factions.attitude_to_player: hostile on sight, unless you carry something Azhmari believes is his

landmarks.name: The Oasis of the Open Palm
landmarks.description: The only reliable water for ninety miles. A ring of palms around a pool whose source nobody has ever traced. The nomads hold it. All trade in the Wastes routes through it.
landmarks.secret: There is a fifth palm, slightly shorter than the others, that was planted the year the Hermit arrived. Nobody saw him plant it.

landmarks.name: The Leviathan Graveyard
landmarks.description: A stretch of sand where the skeletons of sea-beasts surface most readily. Veris's excavation runs through the middle of it. The bones are older than the pyramids beneath them.
landmarks.secret: One skeleton is complete. Most are not. The complete one is not a leviathan — it is something that ate leviathans.

landmarks.name: The Buried Pyramids
landmarks.description: At least eleven. Probably more. Their traps were designed by pharaohs who expected robbers, and they still work.
landmarks.secret: The pyramid closest to the oasis has a door that the sand does not cover. It is a small door, and it is not a trap, and it has never been opened by anyone alive.

landmarks.name: The Bone Reef
landmarks.description: A ridge of fused bone running north to south, tall enough in places to block a loaded camel. Skeletons cluster here.
landmarks.secret: The reef is not a natural formation. It is a wall, built by something, facing the direction of something else.

landmarks.name: Azhmari's Throne
landmarks.description: A buried chamber at the centre of the largest pyramid, where the Sand Prince holds his court of dust and patience.
landmarks.secret: The throne is occupied only part of the time. Where Azhmari goes when he is not on it is a question nobody has survived answering.

regions.music_mood: a single bowed string in a hot wind, with distant percussion that might be a drum or might be a door closing far underground
regions.weather: scorching days, cold nights, sandstorms that arrive without warning and last for hours; the stars at night are brighter than anywhere else in Aelgard
regions.colors: bleached ivory, ochre dust, the pale rose of dawn on bone; a single deep green at the oasis that feels like a hallucination until you taste the water

regions.name: Veilwood
regions.tagline: The forest remembers every footstep. It just doesn't always remember whose.
regions.history_long:
Veilwood was old before the elves found it, and the elves do not like to be reminded of that. Their oldest songs say the forest received them, which is a careful word — not welcomed, not tolerated, but received, the way a deep lake receives a stone. The elves arrived in what must have been late autumn, because all the naming-songs involve falling leaves, and they built their first longhouse in the central clearing where the trees, for reasons never explained, stepped aside.

The Veil Trees are the reason for the region's name, and they are not ordinary trees. They are tall, pale-barked, and their leaves give off a soft light at night that the elves navigate by. The druids say the Veil Trees are listening. The elves say the druids are dramatic. Both are true. The oldest Veil Tree is at the centre of the sacred grove, and she — the pronoun is consistent across every elven language — is called the Veilmother, and she was sleeping.

For most of the elves' history in the forest, the druids and the elves coexisted through a system of mutual avoidance refined to an art. The druids took the deep forest and the burial groves; the elves took the clearings, the hunting grounds, and the river. The two orders met four times a year at the solstices and equinoxes, conducted a ritual so brief that several scholars have missed it while watching, and then returned to ignoring each other until the next one. This worked for a long time.

It stopped working about a generation ago. A young elven ranger — her name has been taken out of the records, which in elven culture is a way of grieving without admitting to grieve — found a grove of Veil Trees dying. Not diseased, not storm-damaged: dying. The druids blamed the elves for overhunting and thinning the undergrowth. The elves blamed the druids for meddling with the Veilmother's sleep. Both were partially right and neither was remotely right. Something older was waking, something that lay beneath the roots and the stories, and it did not care about either order's customs.

The Veilwood Covenant, a treaty hammered out over three seasons of arguments, tried to fix it. The treaty requires any mortal who enters the forest to pass a ranged trial — the elven test of restraint — and to make a small offering at the sacred grove. Most visitors find this reasonable. The treaty has not fixed anything; the dying grove continues to die, and the Veilmother stirred in her roots last winter and has been turning in her sleep ever since.

The thing the player should understand is this: Veilwood is beautiful and Veilwood is dangerous and the two are the same. The light is thin and green because so little sun reaches the forest floor. The unicorns are real but they are not tame. The moss sprites are curious and can be friendly but they can also, if startled, turn an entire clearing to mushroom. And the Veilmother is not a monster, not exactly. She is a sleeping parent whose children are being hurt, and she is waking up, and the question of whether she will distinguish between the hurter and the hurt has never had a good answer.
regions.current_state:
Ranger Lyris holds the border. Tarin the fletcher sells bows in the village and pretends he is not a member of the council. The druids are sealed in the sacred grove and not answering questions. The Elder Druid who corrupted the ritual has been confronted and is dead, or more precisely has been reabsorbed — a druidic fate that the elves find ghoulish and the druids find ordinary. The Veilmother's dreams are turning, and the trees at the edge of the grove are not sleeping any of the three nights a week they are supposed to.

If you pass the trial at the border and walk in, you will be watched. Not always with hostility. The elves are a people who evaluate, and they have not decided about you yet.
regions.geography: A dense forest of enormous trees, broken by occasional clearings. A river runs through it from north to south. The sacred grove sits at the western edge, where the ground slopes up toward the mountains. Light is green and filtered. The forest floor is soft with moss and leaf litter.

factions.name: The Elven Council
factions.description: Six elders who govern the village by consensus. None of them call themselves leaders. All of them are. The council meets in the longhouse at dawn on the days when a decision cannot be postponed.
factions.attitude_to_player: reserved; the council notices everything you do and says nothing about any of it until a year later

factions.name: The Druidic Circle
factions.description: An older order than the elves. They tend the Veil Trees and the sacred grove. They speak seldom and always exactly. They are presently sealed inside their own grove and answering no summons.
factions.attitude_to_player: opaque; if the druids ever speak to you directly, it will be because they have already decided something about you

factions.name: The Wardens of the Boundary
factions.description: Rangers like Lyris who patrol the forest's edge. They enforce the Covenant. They are the visible face of elven authority to outsiders.
factions.attitude_to_player: fair; pass the trial and they will trust your competence, though not necessarily your judgement

landmarks.name: The Sacred Grove
landmarks.description: A clearing ringed by the oldest Veil Trees. The Veilmother is at its centre. The druids live here. Outsiders may enter only during solstice rituals, and not all return.
landmarks.secret: The grove is not round. If you pace its edge, you will return to your starting point having walked a different distance than you started with.

landmarks.name: The Elven Village
landmarks.description: A cluster of longhouses around a central hall, roofed with living leaves that shed at autumn and regrow in spring. The forge is outdoors under an oak older than the village.
landmarks.secret: One longhouse has no door on the outside. It opens only into a small side-room of the central hall, and nobody discusses what it is for.

landmarks.name: The Dying Grove
landmarks.description: A stand of Veil Trees on the eastern slope, visibly pale and losing leaves out of season. The druids forbid approach. The elves forbid speaking of it.
landmarks.secret: The ground beneath the dying trees is warm. Not hot. Warm, like a body.

landmarks.name: Tarin's Fletching House
landmarks.description: A workshop on stilts over the river, where Fletcher Tarin makes elven bows and arrows. He is always there and he is always working.
landmarks.secret: Tarin is on the council and several elves do not know it. He has been for three decades.

regions.music_mood: a harp played slowly with long pauses, the kind of music you would expect to hear behind a door you are not sure you should open
regions.weather: cool in summer, mild in winter, a perpetual soft mist at dawn and dusk; storms arrive filtered and muted through the canopy
regions.colors: deep forest green, pale silver bark, moss emerald, the warm gold of lamp-leaves at dusk; elven cloth in muted earth tones, never bright

regions.name: The Sootworks
regions.tagline: Breathe shallow. Stand on the grate. The forge runs night-and-day.
regions.history_long:
The dwarves came down. That is the phrase they use. Not up, not in — down. They came down from a mountain that is no longer on any map, and they built the Sootworks in the hollow they found when they got to the bottom of the mountain, and they have been building it ever since. The Sootworks is not a city. The Sootworks is a machine that happens to house a city inside itself.

The first forge was lit in the founder's hall and has not gone out in six hundred years. Forgemasters change. The forge does not. Soot-iron — the dwarves' house metal, harder than steel and darker, with a faint grain like wood — can only be smelted at that forge's heat, and the heat is only maintained by feeding the forge the coal of the deep vein, and the deep vein is a seam that runs so far down that the dwarves stopped mapping it three generations ago because the map was useless. You cannot map something that has no bottom. You can only dig.

The gnomes came later. The gnomes are not native. They arrived from the surface during the Spellfire War, refugees from a war the dwarves were not fighting, and they paid their rent in gears. Gnomish clockwork and dwarven metallurgy turned out to be a compatible marriage. Within a century the Sootworks had clockwork sentries patrolling the tunnels, steam trams running between the main chambers, and a mechanical tally-system that tracks ore production to four decimals. The dwarves do not entirely approve of the gnomes. The gnomes do not entirely approve of the dwarves. The Sootworks runs.

The deep vein is the problem. The deep vein has always been the problem. You can ask any dwarf older than sixty and they will tell you that the vein was safer in their grandfather's day, which is what every dwarf has said in every generation back to the founding, which means either the vein is getting steadily worse or the dwarves remember their childhoods too fondly, and it is impossible to tell which. What is not in dispute is that the rock golems have been more active, the lava beasts have been spawning deeper up the shafts, and Vorath — the Warden of the Deep Vein, a construct the dwarves built and then lost the ability to control — has begun refusing to open gates that it used to open daily.

The Soot King is the secret. The dwarves do not speak his name in front of gnomes and the gnomes do not ask. Sealed in a vault below the deepest working shaft, he is older than the Sootworks, and the dwarves found him when they arrived, and their first Forgemaster made a compact with him that bought the dwarves six hundred years of unchallenged tenure. The compact is expiring. Nobody knows the exact date. The dwarves are quietly overproducing soot-iron, banking it against the time when the compact breaks and they have to fight their way out of their own city.

The player arrives in a place that smells, permanently, of hot iron and coal smoke. The air is warm. The grates glow. The dwarves are polite in a curt way that is easy to mistake for hostility. The gnomes are friendly in a frenetic way that is easy to mistake for instability. Neither is wrong. Both are working.
regions.current_state: Forgemaster Brun is working. Smith Hald is working. Engineer Fizz is working on three projects at once and not sleeping. The clockwork sentries on the lower levels have started firing at dwarves and not only at intruders, which is a development the council has not yet publicly acknowledged. Vorath has sealed the lowest working gate. The Soot King is stirring. The compact is expiring, and the dwarves have spent six hundred years preparing for this moment, and now that it is here, they are discovering that preparation and readiness are not the same.
regions.geography: A vast underground complex of tunnels, forge halls, mine shafts, and steam-tram lines. The main concourse is broad enough for a cart. The deep vein descends indefinitely. Ventilation shafts reach the surface at intervals and are always warm. The Sootworks sits roughly east of the Heartlands, accessible through a wide paved tunnel at the Forge Hall entrance.

factions.name: The Forgemaster's Council
factions.description: Seven senior dwarves, led by Forgemaster Brun. They vote. They argue. They make binding decisions by two-thirds majority and stop speaking to each other for months afterward.
factions.attitude_to_player: transactional; complete a contract and they will pay; fail one and they will not speak to you again

factions.name: The Gnomish Engineering Corps
factions.description: Not a formal guild. A cluster of gnome households who trade in clockwork parts and innovation. They keep the trams running. They are terrified of the deep vein and will not go below Level Four for any fee.
factions.attitude_to_player: enthusiastic; hand them a broken mechanism and they will repair it for the pleasure of the puzzle

factions.name: The Deep Vein Miners
factions.description: The dwarves who still work the lowest levels. Older. Quieter. Paid double. They do not eat meals with the other dwarves and they do not sleep in the main dormitories.
factions.attitude_to_player: distant; they answer direct questions with direct answers and volunteer nothing

factions.name: The Bound Scholars
factions.description: A small order of dwarves whose sole task is to read and re-read the Founder's Compact. They keep the original in a sealed case. There are three of them. They are always three of them. When one dies, a new one is appointed within a day.
factions.attitude_to_player: will speak to you only after you have been to the deep vein and come back

landmarks.name: The Founder's Hall
landmarks.description: The central chamber. The first forge burns at the back. The Forgemaster's throne — a low stone bench, nothing ornate — faces the forge. Business is conducted here.
landmarks.secret: The stones of the hall are not quarried. They were already here.

landmarks.name: The Steam Tram Concourse
landmarks.description: The main transit hub. Trams run on regular schedules to the forge halls, the mine shafts, and the surface entrance. The schedule is kept by a gnome who has held the job for forty years.
landmarks.secret: There is a tram line on the board that has no listed stops. It runs once a month. Only three people are permitted to board it.

landmarks.name: The Deep Vein
landmarks.description: The lowest working shaft. Mithril and adamant in the walls. Rock golems in the lift cages. Vorath at the bottom gate.
landmarks.secret: Vorath is not alone down there. When the gate opens, the things behind Vorath are always exactly the same in number.

landmarks.name: The Sealed Vault
landmarks.description: Beneath the deep vein. A door of solid soot-iron, taller than any dwarf. Engraved with the full text of the Founder's Compact. The Soot King sleeps behind it.
landmarks.secret: The door is hinged on the inside.

landmarks.name: The Lantern Archive
landmarks.description: A library of dwarven metallurgical records, kept cold by a ventilation shaft that reaches the glacier above the Sootworks. Most outsiders are not admitted.
landmarks.secret: The archive has a section on gnomish history. Neither dwarves nor gnomes know this.

regions.music_mood: a hammer on an anvil keeping time for a slow wheezing bellows — industry as a lullaby, not a threat
regions.weather: constant warmth, dim orange light from the grates, a permanent haze of coal smoke that the ventilation fails to clear
regions.colors: black iron, coal grey, forge-red glow, brass accents; the gnomes favor green enamel; the dwarves favor nothing but the colors of their metal

regions.name: Moryskah
regions.tagline: You do not come to Moryskah unless you have a reason, and the reason does not always survive the trip.
regions.history_long:
In the oldest maps of Aelgard, the land that is now Moryskah is marked simply as the Low Country, and is not populated. The ground there has always been wet, though the wetness that the original cartographers mapped was not the same wetness that sits over the swamp today. In those days, the Low Country was a seasonal marsh, shallow enough to ford in summer, and a shepherd from the Heartlands might pasture his flock there for weeks and come back with them intact. Something changed. The histories do not agree on when.

What they agree on is that a family arrived — the Malachars — and the family arrived with a writ from a crown that no longer exists, and the writ gave them the Low Country to hold as they saw fit, and the Malachars saw fit to build a castle. Castle Malachar still stands. It stands well. It is the only building in the region whose foundations have not sunk, and the reason is not well understood, but it is understood well enough that the other stone-builders of Aelgard refuse to study it.

The Malachars prospered for eleven generations, and during those generations the marsh deepened, slowly at first and then not slowly. By the ninth generation, the shepherds had stopped coming. By the tenth, the road had been abandoned. By the eleventh, only the Count remained in residence, and his household had become something other than a household, and the village at the castle gate had become a village of people who only came out at night. This is the situation the current church catalogues under the heading The Long Decline, and it declines to investigate further.

Count Malachar — the current one, and the only one, because there has been one Count Malachar for seven centuries, though the dates have been carefully disputed in the family ledgers — sits at the centre of the swamp like a spider at a specific point in a web he has had a very long time to weave. He does not rule, openly. He visits the village. He invites guests. He writes letters. His letters reach the Heartlands and the Sootworks and sometimes the Veilwood. His letters are always answered, because nobody has yet worked out how to refuse him without consequences. The consequences, when they come, are subtle. A kitchen servant in the Heartlands palace develops a cough that will not heal. A caravan from the Sootworks is found on its route with all its drivers alive and unmarked and unable to speak. Nothing that can be proven, and nothing that can be tolerated, and the result is a slow drain of people from every other region into Moryskah, where they arrive and do not leave and are not missed as sharply as they should be.

Father Dorin keeps vigil at the border. He has been keeping vigil for forty years. His task is not to stop people going in — he cannot — but to remember the names of everyone who passes, and to write the names down, and to keep the book. The book is kept in the chapel at the border and the book is kept accurate, and the book is the single most complete record of how many people Moryskah has consumed. Father Dorin does not share the book. If you ask to read it, he will say no. If you ask why, he will say: the book is a list of the dead, and the dead have opinions about who reads about them.

Beneath the Count, and older than the Count, is the Bog Witch Grael, who does not serve the Count and does not oppose the Count, and who brews what Father Dorin cannot. The Bog Witch is what the swamp has instead of a saint. She does not claim the title. She will help you, at prices she names, in the deep part of the marsh where the paths dissolve. Her prices are never money. She will ask you for something she should not need. She will use it. The result will be exactly what she promised, and exactly not what you wanted, and this is the oldest bargain in Moryskah and it has not been broken once.
regions.current_state:
The swamp is restless in a way it has not been restless in decades, and Father Dorin is not sleeping, because the book he keeps has begun to fill faster than it was filling five years ago, and because his daughter, who went into the swamp to apprentice with Nira the apothecary, has not sent word in a month, and because a letter came from the Count, addressed to Father Dorin personally, and sealed in black wax, and Father Dorin has not opened it.

The Slayer Tower is busy. Varrek is not assigning the easy tasks anymore. There is a quiet understanding, among the tower regulars, that something is stirring in Castle Malachar that has not stirred in a long time, and that the Count is gathering what he has been owed, and that he is going to call in a debt.
regions.geography: A vast swamp broken by dry islands of twisted trees, threaded by raised causeways and hidden paths. Two notable elevations: the Slayer Tower in the north, built on a rock outcrop; and Castle Malachar in the south, built on whatever it is built on, which is not rock. A village clearing sits at the crossroads, lit by lantern oil rather than wood fires because the wood does not dry.

factions.name: Count Malachar's Household
factions.description: The Count, his seneschal, a handful of vampyre nobles who dine at the castle, and the Long-Serving — a class of servant who has lived at the castle for so long that their mortality has become theoretical. The household corresponds with every regional capital and is received politely everywhere.
factions.attitude_to_player: impeccably courteous until it is no longer necessary to be courteous

factions.name: Father Dorin's Vigil
factions.description: An order of one, technically, though three acolytes assist. They keep the border chapel, maintain the book, and perform last rites on the edge of the swamp for those who walked in and are known not to be coming out.
factions.attitude_to_player: direct, tired, and grateful for any help; will warn you honestly

factions.name: The Slayer Tower
factions.description: An independent combat training outpost run by Slayer Master Varrek. Technically answerable to no region. Draws its clientele from everywhere. Varrek himself is scarred enough that his face is a kind of credential.
factions.attitude_to_player: professional; assigns tasks you are capable of and not more

factions.name: Bog Witch Grael
factions.description: One woman in a hut at the deepest accessible point of the swamp. She is not a faction. The swamp treats her as one.
factions.attitude_to_player: transactional; her prices are never stated in coin, and you will know the price only when it has been paid

landmarks.name: Castle Malachar
landmarks.description: The Count's seat. A black-stoned castle whose foundations do not sink. Ringed by dead willow. Invitations are required to enter through the main gate; a number of informal entrances exist and are watched.
landmarks.secret: The Count's library contains a shelf of books written by people who are not currently remembered as having existed. Their biographies are on the facing shelf.

landmarks.name: The Border Chapel
landmarks.description: A small stone chapel at the northern edge of the swamp. A single candle is kept burning. The book is kept in a locked box under the altar.
landmarks.secret: The chapel's bell was cast in the Heartlands and carried here by one man on foot, and the man is on the list.

landmarks.name: The Slayer Tower
landmarks.description: A circular stone tower built on a rock outcrop. Four floors. The higher you climb, the worse the company.
landmarks.secret: The top floor is sealed. Varrek claims it is under renovation. He has claimed this for seventeen years.

landmarks.name: The Witch's Hut
landmarks.description: A thatched hut balanced on four stilts in the deep swamp. Smoke rises from the chimney at all hours. The witch is always there.
landmarks.secret: The hut can be found only by people who have business with the witch. The paths rearrange for those who don't.

landmarks.name: The Raided Village
landmarks.description: A small settlement south of the village proper, recently emptied. Vampyre nobles have been taking residents. Father Dorin's book has the names.
landmarks.secret: One cottage is still inhabited. The inhabitant has been inhabiting it for three hundred years and does not answer the door.

regions.music_mood: a low, slow cello with irregular drops of water keeping a time the listener cannot quite find, and a woman humming once, very far off
regions.weather: permanently overcast, cold and damp, mist rising from the water at dawn and refusing to burn off by noon, occasional rain that does not feel like cleansing
regions.colors: black water, moss green, bone white where the trees have died, the deep red of the Count's signet and of nothing else

regions.name: The Inkweald
regions.tagline: A door. You recognise it. You do not remember opening it. The door is open.
regions.history_long:
The Inkweald is not a forest the way Veilwood is a forest. The Inkweald is a place that has agreed, provisionally, to be a forest for as long as you are looking at it. The trees are tall and pale and they move when you are not watching, and the ground underfoot is either moss or is waiting patiently to be moss, and the air is warm and close in a way that is pleasant until you notice that there is no weather beyond the canopy because there is no beyond the canopy — the sky is not there, only another layer of trees.

No one built the Inkweald. Several people, over the millennia, have claimed to have found it, and their claims have never been quite consistent with each other: one scholar puts the discovery at three hundred years ago, another at three thousand, a third at last Tuesday. The discrepancy is not error. The Inkweald is not a place where time behaves. The scholars who study it have learned to record their observations immediately, because what they remember about their observations will not match what they wrote down, and the writing is more reliable, though not entirely.

The Lucid Keepers are the order who have built a barrier at the Inkweald's edge and who hold it there by constant attention. Yara is the senior Keeper at the current boundary camp. The camp has been at that spot for a variable amount of time. Yara has been at the camp for longer than the camp has existed. This is not a contradiction inside the Keepers' doctrine, which distinguishes between where a thing is and when a thing is, and which holds that the Inkweald does not fully commit to either.

The creatures of the Inkweald are not creatures the way creatures are elsewhere. A dream wisp is a mote of light that has a personality. A thought stalker is something that hunts by sensing you thinking. A mirror golem is what your reflection would be if your reflection got tired of the arrangement. The danger is real: a dream wisp will ignore you, but a thought stalker will kill you, and an ink horror will reformat the part of the forest you were standing in. The danger is also uneven, because the Inkweald's rules change depending on how long you have been inside it, and what you have been carrying, and whether you dreamed about the forest before you arrived.

The Hollow Choir is somewhere inside. Deep inside. The Hollow Choir sings. The song, when it reaches the boundary camp, arrives as a faint pressure at the back of the head rather than a sound, and it reshapes the part of the forest that hears it, and the Keepers have been reinforcing the barrier for what Yara calls recently, which is a word that means less here than it means elsewhere. The Conductor leads the choir. Nobody has seen the Conductor and come back and remembered seeing the Conductor at the same time.

This is what the Inkweald is. It is not a region. It is a permission the world extends to a certain class of impossibility, and the permission is being tested, and the Keepers are the membrane, and the membrane is thinning. You enter at your own risk, and the risk is not that you will be killed, because death is a clean outcome and the Inkweald prefers unclean ones. You enter, instead, at the risk that you will come out changed in a way that is correct for the Inkweald and wrong for the life you used to live.
regions.current_state: Yara is not sleeping. The barrier holds. The barrier is not as thick as it was. A scribe from the boundary camp woke up last week speaking a language that nobody could place, and then, halfway through breakfast, stopped speaking it, and has not since been able to describe it. The scribe is fine. The scribe is writing the usual reports. The Keepers have noted the incident and continue.
regions.geography: An enclosed forest that behaves like enclosed space even though it visibly stretches to the horizon. A boundary camp at the edge where mortals can still make stable shelter. Deeper in, the geometry fails: paths loop, trees duplicate, clearings appear in places they were not before. The Resonance Chamber — where the Hollow Choir sings — is somewhere at the centre, if there is a centre.

factions.name: The Lucid Keepers
factions.description: A small order of scholars and sealers who maintain the barrier between the Inkweald and everywhere else. They take rotating shifts that are measured not in hours but in attention. Yara is the senior Keeper at the present boundary camp.
factions.attitude_to_player: helpful and specific; they will tell you exactly what is safe and exactly what is not, and they are often right

factions.name: The Scribes' Grove
factions.description: A sub-order of Keepers who spend their shifts transcribing everything that happens at the camp, because memory is not reliable here. Their records are kept in a vault that is kept in the Heartlands because the Inkweald occasionally reaches into its own camp and rewrites things.
factions.attitude_to_player: distracted; always writing; friendly when interrupted, which is often

factions.name: The Sleepwalkers
factions.description: Not a faction in any willful sense. People who went too deep and are now walking the Inkweald without waking. There are many. The Keepers try to retrieve them. Few return, and of those who return, few remain retrieved.
factions.attitude_to_player: passively dangerous; will walk toward you; will swing at you if you get close; show no recognition

factions.name: The Hollow Choir
factions.description: The singers at the heart. They are not individuals, or they are many individuals acting as one, or the distinction is a category error. The Conductor leads.
factions.attitude_to_player: indifferent at distance, directly malevolent at proximity, and neither impression is stable

landmarks.name: The Boundary Camp
landmarks.description: A ring of lanterns and canvas at the Inkweald's edge. Yara's tent. A small bank vault. A cookfire that does not go out because if it does, the boundary thins.
landmarks.secret: The cookfire has not gone out in eleven generations. It has been moved exactly twice. Neither move is in the official record.

landmarks.name: The Mirror Pond
landmarks.description: A pool, ankle-deep, at a clearing about a day's walk in. It reflects clearly. It does not always reflect truly.
landmarks.secret: The pond answers questions you ask of your reflection, but only once per visitor per lifetime, and only if the question is one the reflection did not expect.

landmarks.name: The Scribe Grove
landmarks.description: A stand of pale trees whose bark can be peeled off as parchment. The parchment records what is written on it accurately. It also, occasionally, records things that were not written on it.
landmarks.secret: A parchment peeled from the oldest tree will tell you what you most need to hear. It will not tell you what you most want to hear.

landmarks.name: The Resonance Chamber
landmarks.description: A chamber at the centre, if there is a centre. The Conductor leads the choir here. The chamber's walls are made of a substance that is neither wood nor stone and that hums when touched.
landmarks.secret: The chamber's floor has a door in it. The door opens downward. What is below the floor has no description on record.

landmarks.name: The Paradox Rabbit Warren
landmarks.description: A meadow just past the boundary where small, shifting creatures dart between burrows that are not always in the same place. Their fur grants a single doubled task to anyone who carries it.
landmarks.secret: The rabbits are the same rabbit. Always. Everywhere.

regions.music_mood: a bell ringing underwater, a voice singing the third note of a scale without the other notes, the hush of a library that is empty and was never not empty
regions.weather: no weather. A perpetual warm dim. Lights seem closer than they are. Sound reaches the camp late, or early, or not
regions.colors: bruise violet, pale ink, the cream of old parchment, a green that is not a plant green, and a single thread of silver visible in everything if you look right

regions.name: Saltbrine Reach
regions.tagline: The tide comes in twice a day and takes something each time, and nobody keeps count anymore.
regions.history_long:
Saltbrine Reach is a curve of coast, a crescent harbour, a string of fishing villages, and a long-running argument with the sea. The argument has been running since the first Reach settlement was founded, by fishermen whose names have not survived, on a beach where a freshwater stream met the salt water and the mackerel schooled thick enough to catch with your hands. That beach is gone now. The sea took it. The settlement moved inland, and then inland again, and the current harbour is the sixth to have held the Reach's name, and the seventh will be built, in time, because it always is.

The Reach is a pirate coast in the careful, formal sense that the crown has never been able to enforce its ordinary laws here. The Harbourmaster — currently Cole, a stressed and competent man who has held the post for twenty years — is a crown appointee, but his actual authority is limited by the fact that he does not pay the dockworkers' wages and cannot enforce any law that would interrupt the fishing. The dockworkers' wages are paid by the fishing cooperatives, which are paid by the markets, which are paid, in the end, by the guilds of the Heartlands, who buy Reach-caught salmon and lobster and swordfish in quantities the Reach could not replace with any other buyer. This is the polity. Cole manages it. He does not enforce it.

The pirates, therefore, are tolerated. Not by Cole, but by the economics. A small cove at the eastern edge of the harbour holds a settlement that no map shows and everyone knows the location of, and the pirates there pay a tithe to the fishing cooperatives in exchange for not robbing the cooperatives' boats. When the tithe is paid, the pirates rob other boats — trade vessels from further down the coast, slow galleons out of kingdoms the Reach does not recognise. When the tithe is not paid, for whatever reason, the pirates rob the cooperatives, and the cooperatives pay the tithe again. This system is stable. Cole would like to dismantle it. He has not been given the force to do so, and he has begun to suspect that the force has been withheld on purpose.

The sea itself is the other party to the Reach's long argument. The sea gives. The sea takes. The oyster beds at the northern end of the harbour produce pearls that are sold inland for hundreds of coins each, and two boats a year are lost in the oyster channels. The deep-water grounds past the breakwater yield swordfish and shark, and the siren rocks just past them yield shipwrecks on the schedule of one every eight or nine years. None of this is unusual for a fishing coast. What is unusual, what has begun to be unusual, is that the sea has started to sing.

The singing has been audible for about a year. Fishmonger Mara noticed it first: a low note at the bottom of the harbour tide, carrying up through the hulls of the moored boats on a calm night. She asked three other fishermen, and they had all heard it and had all assumed they were imagining it. They were not imagining it. Something is under the harbour. The oldest among the fishermen, a man named Petric who will not speak his surname, says it is the Kraken, and that the Kraken used to live farther out, and that it has come closer because something has changed, and that nothing good ever comes of the Kraken coming closer. Petric has been saying this for forty years and has been wrong for thirty-nine of them. He is not wrong now.
regions.current_state: The pirates blockaded the harbour last season and were driven off by a concerted effort that cost three boats and two captains. The blockade has not reformed, but the pirate cove is rebuilding, and the cooperatives are paying a higher tithe than they were. Mara has set up a fishing tackle and food stall at the dock and is quietly organising a delegation to travel to Moryskah to consult the Bog Witch on the singing. Harbourmaster Cole is three nights into a week without sleep and has a stack of unanswered letters from the crown on his desk. The Kraken is closer. The tide comes in twice a day.
regions.geography: A curved harbour protected by a long stone breakwater. Beach to either side. Fishing villages running up the coast, each with its own jetty. A pirate cove to the east, informally. Deep water past the breakwater, where the siren rocks are. The harbour town proper has a small market, a range, a bank, and Mara's tackle shop.

factions.name: The Fishing Cooperatives
factions.description: The actual government of the Reach in all practical senses. A consortium of boat captains and fishmongers who pay the dockworkers and negotiate with the pirates. Mara is on the inner council.
factions.attitude_to_player: friendly if you bring them fish, transactional if you don't, loyal if you help them with a problem they name themselves

factions.name: The Harbourmaster's Office
factions.description: Cole, two clerks, and a ledger that does not balance. The Office collects docking fees and issues writs. Its actual authority is narrow. Its informal role is to absorb blame for anything the cooperatives do not want to be blamed for.
factions.attitude_to_player: grateful for competence, quietly desperate for allies

factions.name: The Pirate Cove
factions.description: A shanty settlement of buccaneers, privateers, and assorted unlicensed seafarers. Led informally by a rotating cast of captains who do not publicly acknowledge a leader but who all answer the same horn.
factions.attitude_to_player: hostile on principle, negotiable in practice, capable of hiring you if you prove competent and discreet

factions.name: The Deep-Water Watchers
factions.description: A handful of old fishermen, Petric chief among them, who have begun meeting at dusk on the breakwater and not speaking, and watching the water.
factions.attitude_to_player: they will not speak to you until you have heard the singing; after that, they will speak to nobody else

landmarks.name: Saltbrine Harbour
landmarks.description: The main dock. Five jetties. A bank. A range for cooking fresh catch at dockside. Mara's stall is nearest the market.
landmarks.secret: The north jetty's third piling is older than the others by about two hundred years. Nobody knows why it was reused.

landmarks.name: The Pirate Cove
landmarks.description: A hidden harbour to the east, accessible by a tide-dependent channel. A cluster of shanties, a galleon in permanent dry dock, a tavern.
landmarks.secret: The galleon's hull is not wood. Every timber of it was replaced, plank by plank, over the last hundred years, and the original ship it was is no longer present in any meaningful way, but the name on the stern has not changed.

landmarks.name: The Siren Rocks
landmarks.description: A cluster of jagged black rocks past the breakwater. The sirens nest here. Ships that sail close do not always return.
landmarks.secret: The rocks are hollow. The sirens live inside them, not on them. The hollows are large.

landmarks.name: The Oyster Beds
landmarks.description: A shallow bed at the northern end of the harbour, farmed by the cooperatives. Pearls. Sea glass. Occasional coral fragments.
landmarks.secret: One of the oysters — no one knows which — has been growing continuously for a century. Its pearl is a relic.

landmarks.name: Mara's Stall
landmarks.description: A plank counter by the dock. Raw fish on ice. Cooked fish for travellers. A stove. A ledger.
landmarks.secret: The ledger records not only sales but everything Mara has heard from the sailors who bought from her, and it is kept in code only the cooperatives can read.

regions.music_mood: a concertina and a fiddle over a slow swell of cello — a harbour song that remembers drowned singers without dwelling on them
regions.weather: salt wind year-round, fog at dawn, hot summer afternoons, winter storms that can rearrange the jetties
regions.colors: grey-blue sea, wet dark wood, pale rope, copper verdigris on the bells, the red of the pirate cove's flags; gull white everywhere

regions.name: The Glass Desert
regions.tagline: The sand here is half-melted. Do not ask what melted it.
regions.history_long:
The Glass Desert is what the east became after the Last Fire. Before the Last Fire, the histories say, it was something else — plains, perhaps, or lightly wooded hills — and the Last Fire burned it to nothing, and the nothing cooled, and the cooled nothing fused, and that is why the sand here crunches rather than shifts, and why the dunes glitter, and why a traveller without a veil will burn her eyes out inside a day. The Last Fire is a vague event in the historical record. Some sources put it at five thousand years ago. Some put it at fifteen thousand. All of them are guessing. None of them are quite willing to say what the Fire was.

Veldrak is what the Fire was. Not the only thing — the Last Fire was a confluence — but Veldrak was the largest part of it. Veldrak is a dragon, the last dragon, and the sleep that holds Veldrak now is the reason the Glass Desert is a place where people can enter at all. The sleep was not cheap. The Crystal Sage Orin will tell you about it in slow, careful sentences, and when he talks about the sleep he uses a possessive pronoun, which is itself a clue about how the sleep is maintained: not collectively, not institutionally, but personally, by a small order of sages who have each held a fragment of the binding in their bodies for as long as they lived, and who trained their successors before they died, and whose chain is now eleven centuries old and is not as unbroken as the histories say.

The Glass Tyrant is older than Veldrak. The Tyrant was here before the Fire. It is a being of living crystal — a creature, not a construct — and its relationship to the dragon is unclear to every living scholar. The Tyrant does not sleep. The Tyrant rules the deep crystal arenas at the desert's centre. It does not attack travellers unless travellers attack it. When travellers attack it, it attacks back. The survival rate is low. The Tyrant has existed, by every available measure, for longer than any other single living thing on Aelgard.

The Fight Caves and the Inferno sit beneath the desert. They are not natural formations. They were built, by whom nobody knows, as a training ground or an arena or a trap, depending on which theory you find most plausible. Ascending the Caves awards the Cape of the Inner Fire, which is the surface world's most durable prestige item. Ascending the Inferno awards the Infernal Cape, which is the same thing but for people who have finished ascending the Caves. Nobody has ascended both without a great deal of help, and nobody has done either without practice, and nobody has practiced without dying repeatedly, and this is considered by the sages to be the system working as intended.

The TzHaar live in the fight caves. The word is their own, not a loan. They are older than the elves and they may be older than the dragons, and their relationship to the crystal is intimate: they are not made of crystal but they are not independent of it either. They forge obsidian into weapons and armour and they sell it, through Merchant Zel at the outpost, at prices calibrated to the wealth of the desperate. Their conversation is limited. Their respect is earned only in their arena, and the respect is worth earning.

This is the endgame region. It is not endgame because the sages made it so. It is endgame because you cannot come here without having survived everything else.
regions.current_state: Orin is at the outpost and is older than he was last year, which is the natural direction, but also older than he should be, which is the unnatural one. He has been dreaming the same dream for eleven weeks, and the dream is about Veldrak's eye opening. Zel is busy. The Fight Caves have had twelve successful ascents this month, which is a record. The Inferno has had one. Veldrak is still asleep. The sleep is thinner.
regions.geography: A wasteland of fused sand and crystal formations, with occasional sharp glass-rock outcroppings. A single outpost at the western edge, sheltered by overhangs. Deeper in, the arenas: the Crystal Caverns (Wyrm country), the Glass Tyrant's Arena, the Fight Caves and Inferno entrances, Veldrak's buried chamber. The sun overhead is white and the sun on the glass is whiter.

factions.name: The Crystal Sages
factions.description: An order of eleven, always eleven. Orin is the current senior. Each holds a fragment of Veldrak's binding. When one dies, a successor is chosen. The order does not govern and is not consulted by any crown, but any serious action in the desert routes through them eventually.
factions.attitude_to_player: patient, specific, willing to answer questions that have a purpose, and silent about questions that do not

factions.name: The TzHaar
factions.description: A people of fire-born warriors who live in the caves beneath the desert. They forge obsidian and run the Fight Caves. They do not trade with any surface culture except through Zel.
factions.attitude_to_player: indifferent until you enter the caves; respectful only if you ascend

factions.name: Merchant Zel's Exchange
factions.description: Zel herself, three assistants, and a warehouse at the outpost. Zel trades crystal shards, glass sand, prism lenses, and TzHaar obsidian. She is not a TzHaar but she speaks their trading dialect.
factions.attitude_to_player: professional; will buy anything from the desert at market rates and sell you anything the TzHaar release to the surface

factions.name: Orin's Listeners
factions.description: Not a formal group. A handful of travellers who have stayed longer at the outpost than their business required, and who now sit with Orin in the evenings while he talks. They remember what he tells them. The Sages do not officially sanction them, but they do not stop them.
factions.attitude_to_player: will nod to you if you sit long enough to be recognised

landmarks.name: The Glass Desert Outpost
landmarks.description: A cluster of stone buildings under the lee of a large crystal outcrop. A bank. Zel's exchange. A water cistern fed by a spring that should not exist where it exists.
landmarks.secret: The cistern's spring comes from a depth the Sages have mapped to a door they have never opened.

landmarks.name: The Crystal Caverns
landmarks.description: A labyrinth of glass-walled tunnels where the Crystal Wyrm lives. Sealed. Accessible only after completing the Glass Prophecy.
landmarks.secret: The Wyrm is not alone. There is an empty bed in the caverns, nearby. It has been empty for a long time. It is not shaped like the Wyrm's bed.

landmarks.name: The Glass Tyrant's Arena
landmarks.description: A broad depression in the desert floor where the Tyrant holds court. The ground is smooth. The walls are faceted. The Tyrant does not leave.
landmarks.secret: The Tyrant's phases — melee, ranged, magic — match the phases of something very old, and the Sages recognise the pattern but have not said aloud what it is.

landmarks.name: The Fight Caves
landmarks.description: A spiral descent into sixty-three waves of TzHaar combat. Reaching the bottom awards the Cape of the Inner Fire.
landmarks.secret: The caves have sixty-four waves. The last is not counted because nobody has seen it.

landmarks.name: The Inferno
landmarks.description: A sealed lower descent. Sixty-nine waves. Ascending awards the Infernal Cape.
landmarks.secret: The Inferno was not built. It was found.

landmarks.name: The Dragon Gate
landmarks.description: A doorway at the centre of the desert that opens only when the four regional keys are brought. Beyond it: Veldrak's chamber.
landmarks.secret: The gate is older than the dragon behind it. This is the Sages' private worry.

regions.music_mood: a high sustained chime over a ground drone that never resolves — beauty that refuses to be consoling
regions.weather: blinding heat by day, sharp cold at night, occasional crystal-dust storms that can score leather; no rain, ever
regions.colors: white sand, prism colors where the sun catches a facet, a deep rose at dawn, the rare green of living crystal; the ground blazes at noon and burns with the colour of a knife at dusk

regions.name: The Wilds
regions.tagline: The rules that keep you alive elsewhere are suggestions here. The suggestions are not taken.
regions.history_long:
The Wilds are what the north became when the crown stopped enforcing the north. This happened gradually and then all at once. The gradual part was the long erosion of royal authority that followed the Spellfire War, when the standing garrisons at the northern frontier stopped being paid reliably and the patrols got shorter and the patrols stopped, and brigands moved in, and then brigands moved out because there was nothing in the Wilds to steal that was worth the risk, and then the brigands came back because the Wilds had grown things that were worth exactly the risk required to take them.

The all-at-once part was the Kingsfall. A regent, lesser crown, three decades ago, attempted to re-establish the northern garrisons. He led an expedition north in the spring, with a full company and a banner and two wagons of salt pork, and the expedition returned in autumn without the regent, without the banner, and with three men who would not speak of what had happened. The salt pork was intact. The crown has not sent another expedition. The Wilds have been the Wilds, officially and finally, since the day the three silent men walked back to the Heartlands gate.

What the Wilds are, practically, is a zone of suspended law. The crown does not enforce its statutes here. The guilds do not enforce their codes. There is no sheriff, no bailiff, no writ. Anyone who enters is subject to attack by anyone else who enters. This is not a metaphor. The rule is literal. The signs at the border say so, in plain script, and the signs are updated annually because the weather and the wolves and the occasional disagreement burn the old signs.

The value of the Wilds is in what grows in them precisely because nobody polices them. Revenants — the ghosts of an older, bloodier war — roam the inner ruins and drop weapons that are among the most powerful in Aelgard, but only inside the Wilds. Herbs grow here that grow nowhere else. Tree species flourish because no forester culls them. Pure essence veins run through the north crater, and they yield three times the essence of any similar vein in the settled regions. The Chaos Altar — a broken shrine at the centre of the southern Wilds — accepts bones and returns prayer merit at a rate no sanctioned altar matches. All of this is available for the taking. All of this is available for the taking by anyone, which means you will not be taking it alone, and the other takers are armed.

Callisto, Venenatis, and Vet'ion are the three great beasts of the inner Wilds. Callisto is a bear older than the Kingsfall. Venenatis is a spider whose web spans a ruin. Vet'ion is a revenant king in a broken crypt. Each of them can be killed by a prepared party. Each of them drops items that can be sold to pay for a year's equipment. Each of them sits in a zone where other players are actively hunting other players, and the other players are often better prepared, and this is the trade the Wilds offers: you can have more than you could have anywhere else, and you can have less. The distribution is not equitable. It is honest.

The Revenant King is the rumour. The Wilds' deepest secret. A crown, somewhere, in a ruin nobody has catalogued, worn by a revenant who was once, maybe, the lost regent. The crown, if recovered, is a prestige item whose effect is unambiguous in the Wilds and trivial outside them: twenty percent damage bonus inside the border, nothing outside. It is the most valuable item nobody has confirmed the existence of. It is being searched for. The searching has started wars.
regions.current_state: The northern border signs have been replaced recently. Krystilia, the wilderness slayer master, sits at a small desk at the edge of the zone and assigns tasks to those foolish enough to accept them. The bounty hunter system, run by an NPC at the same desk, pays out in emblems for killing other hunters. The pirate cove has started sending raiding parties overland into the southern Wilds. Larran's chest, somewhere in the old ruins, has been found twice this month. The Revenant King has not been found.
regions.geography: A broad, unpoliced expanse north of the Heartlands. Dry grasslands scoured by wind. Broken ruins, pre-Kingsfall. A lava pit near the centre. A crater of pure essence veins. Caves and crypts throughout. No roads are maintained. No bridges are repaired. The terrain is walkable but not welcoming.

factions.name: Krystilia's Wilderness Slayer Lodge
factions.description: Krystilia assigns wilderness-only tasks from a desk that is always at the border. The tasks pay better than regular slayer and the monsters are worse.
factions.attitude_to_player: neutral; assigns tasks by skill, warns you honestly about danger, does not attend funerals

factions.name: The Bounty Hunters
factions.description: An informal network of combat-trained adventurers who have agreed, through the Bounty Hunter system, to hunt each other for emblems. Most bounty hunters know each other professionally.
factions.attitude_to_player: cooperative if you've earned emblems, predatory if you haven't

factions.name: The Revenant Packs
factions.description: The risen dead of the Kingsfall and older. Armoured. Armed. They drop the wilderness weapons, and they drop them only here.
factions.attitude_to_player: aggressive; they will engage anyone, including each other, and they will prioritise whoever is carrying the most

factions.name: The Wilds' Three
factions.description: Callisto the bear, Venenatis the spider, Vet'ion the revenant king. Independent beasts. Territorial.
factions.attitude_to_player: territorial, each in their own zone; none of them care who killed the last adventurer who tried

landmarks.name: The Abandoned Ruins
landmarks.description: The fallen garrison at the centre of the Wilds. Stones scattered across ten acres. Revenants patrol the courtyards. Rain water pools in the flagstones.
landmarks.secret: One watchtower is still intact. The door is barred from inside.

landmarks.name: The Lava Pit
landmarks.description: A natural lava pool at the centre-north. The heat keeps the snow off for a quarter mile around. Lava beasts nest in it.
landmarks.secret: The pit has a lip. Standing on the lip, you can see further into the Wilds than any map shows.

landmarks.name: The Chaos Altar
landmarks.description: A broken shrine on a low rise in the southern Wilds. Bones placed here yield a sevenfold prayer bonus when consumed. Nearby, there is always someone waiting for someone else to finish.
landmarks.secret: The altar stone is the same stone as the Last Light chapel's altar in the Heartlands. The provenance is not documented.

landmarks.name: Larran's Chest
landmarks.description: A locked iron chest, usually somewhere in the ruins, opened by keys dropped from wilderness slayer tasks. Contents are valuable and variable.
landmarks.secret: The chest moves. Not between uses — during them.

landmarks.name: The Revenant King's Crypt
landmarks.description: Unconfirmed. Rumoured. A sealed burial chamber at the deepest point of the northern ruins, where the Revenant King wears a crown.
landmarks.secret: The door to the crypt is not locked. The door has not been opened because the three people who reached it in the last fifty years chose not to open it, and none of them have explained their decision.

regions.music_mood: a wind over open ground, an irregular drum, a single voice that begins a melody and does not finish it; the sound of a place that was meant to be inhabited and isn't
regions.weather: cold winds year-round, sudden fogs, dry thunder in summer, hard snow in winter that buries the lower ruins
regions.colors: dead grass gold, old stone grey, the black of burnt timbers, the red of fresh blood on snow; at night, the lava pit glows orange across the whole central basin

bosses.name: Forgefather Duran
bosses.bestiary:
Duran was a Heartlands smith, and not a bad one — competent enough to be promoted, weak enough to resent the promotion, and stubborn enough to turn that resentment into a project. He was given the Heartlands Smithing Guild in his forty-second year, and he declined to run it the way the previous Forgefather had run it, and within five years he had left the guild under circumstances the guild's records describe as mutually agreed and which were not.

He went north. He took his hammer and his apprentice, and the apprentice is still missing, and the hammer is now the burning hammer which Duran wields today as the primary feature of his combat. He built a private forge in the hills above the Heartlands and he began to smith weapons that he sold to anyone who asked, at prices that undercut the guild, and he did this until the guild sent a delegation to ask him to stop, and the delegation did not return, and a second delegation was not sent.

The burning hammer is the Forgefather's signature. It is soot-iron, forged by him personally, and it holds heat at a temperature that should have melted it a long time ago. How he maintains this is not known. Several Heartlands scholars have theorised that he bargained with something at the Sootworks for the privilege, and that the bargain has since come due in ways that are showing. Duran's face is thinner than it was. His apprentice is long gone. The forge behind him is lit by no visible fire.

Players encounter him in the hills and find him willing, almost eager, to fight. He does not taunt. He does not bargain. He swings, and the hammer swings with a weight that is heavier than iron should be, and a swing catches fire as it lands. His armour is heavy and his skin is bright-red where the heat of the hammer has reached it over the years. He is, in the strict sense, still a human being. He is what human beings become when they build something in anger and will not stop tending it.

Survive him with a piercing weapon — stab through the armour gaps at the joints, because slash will not get through and crush will not do enough damage fast enough. Melee gloves and adamant gear are standard. He drops his hammer occasionally, and the hammer cools within a minute of his death, and the hammer can then be taken.
bosses.kill_cry: He says the name of his apprentice. You do not know who that is.

bosses.name: The Evil Chef
bosses.bestiary:
The Culinaromancer was a title, once — an honorific for the senior chef of the Heartlands Grand Hall, back when the Hall held feasts for six hundred and the kitchens ran three shifts. The last Culinaromancer was a woman named Vessa, who retired into a small private kitchen after the court dissolved, and who vanished from that kitchen one winter, leaving a pot on the stove that was still warm when her assistant found it two weeks later.

The Evil Chef is what came back. Not Vessa. Not entirely not Vessa. The kitchen stayed warm for a decade. Then there was a soup, in the kitchen, that had not been made, and the soup was good, and the soup was tasted and found to contain ingredients that had not been brought to the Hall in a hundred years, and the kitchen was sealed. The Evil Chef emerged from the kitchen some time after that, by a route nobody saw, and began haunting the Grand Hall.

The Evil Chef's combat is a three-course meal. The first phase is Soup: the Chef hurls ladles of scalding broth, and the floor fills with steaming puddles that must be stepped around rather than through. The second phase is the Main: the Chef wields a cleaver the size of a door and attacks in heavy arcs that can be parried but must be timed. The third phase is Dessert: the Chef produces a pastry — a glossy, dark thing, iced with something that is not icing — and hurls it, and the pastry explodes, and the explosion spreads an effect across the room that drains any buff or potion the player is relying on.

The Chef is armoured in an apron. The apron is not ordinary cloth. The Chef is slow. The Chef is not intelligent in the ordinary sense — it does not strategise — but it does recognise food in an adventurer's inventory, and the Chef will prioritise attacks on any adventurer who is holding something edible. There is an obvious tactical consequence. Come hungry.

Defeat awards the Culinaromancer Gloves, which are the best melee gloves available before Barrows-tier equipment, and access to the Grand Hall, which restores the Heartlands' central teleport hub. The Evil Chef drops the gloves from a severed hand, and the severed hand is Vessa's hand, and the Lamplighters at the Chapel of the Last Light will, if asked, tell the player how to bury it.
bosses.kill_cry: The kitchen falls silent. Somewhere, a pot stops boiling.

bosses.name: Azhmari, The Sand Prince
bosses.bestiary:
Azhmari was the last-but-one pharaoh of Kherem, and he is the reason Kherem is not a pharaohdom anymore. The histories are thin. The archaeologists reconstruct them from stela fragments and from the Hermit's occasional answers. What is consistent across sources is this: Azhmari refused to die, and he refused to die by means that were specific and elaborate and that worked, in that he is not dead, but that did not work, in that he is also not alive, and he has been occupying the gap between those two states for more centuries than the crown of the Heartlands has existed.

His tomb is the largest pyramid in the Wastes. Inside is his throne. On the throne he sits when he sits at all. He does not always sit. Where he goes when he is not sitting is the first of the three questions the Hermit will answer if a player brings the right bone, and the answer, the Hermit reports, is a word Azhmari himself taught the Hermit to use for the destination, and the word is not translated.

When fought, Azhmari is airborne at medium range. He carries no weapon. His magic is ancient — a pharaohnic style that has not been practiced in any surface court in recorded history — and the spells are slow but certain. A Sandstorm spell that he casts near the end of his first health bar will fill the throne room with grit so thick that melee combat becomes impossible, and this is his signal that the second phase is underway, in which he descends to the ground and fights with a staff he produces from the sand itself.

He is weak to ranged. The ancient magic shields against melee at a level that no contemporary weapon can punch through. Arrows ignore the shielding — the shielding was designed against armies that did not have archers of any competence, and the design has not been updated. Magic bounces. Spears work only if thrown.
