Bows work reliably.

His loot is dense and varied: his crown, a golden thing that hums; the Sandstorm Staff, which casts desert lightning; the Bone Cleaver, a great axe made from a leviathan's jaw. The crown is the prize. It sits on his head during the fight and comes free when he falls, and it is the only pharaoh's crown in Aelgard that is currently outside a museum and that contains a signal still reaching its original sender.
bosses.kill_cry: He whispers something in the old Kherem language. The Hermit, far away at the oasis, stands up.

bosses.name: The Bog Hydra
bosses.bestiary:
The Bog Hydra lives at the border of the Wastes and Moryskah, where the salt ground gives way to black water, in a pool fed by a spring that comes up through sand and runs out as brackish marsh. It has three heads. The heads are not in agreement about anything except hunger. It has been in this pool for longer than the current generation of nomads has been alive, and the nomads navigate around it, and the archaeologists will not go to that corner of the dig site on principle.

The middle head spits acid at range. The left head bites. The right head, a smaller head that looks almost apologetic, breathes a poison that lingers on the ground for three or four seconds after the breath, long enough to trap a player who dodged the initial exhalation. The three heads do not coordinate but they do alternate, and the alternation follows a pattern that a careful fighter can learn inside the first minute of the fight.

It is weak to magic. The thick hide deflects arrows and absorbs melee strikes; fire and ice break through the scales in ways that physical weapons do not. It drops hydra scales at a moderate rate, and the scales are the core component of hydra leather body, which is the best ranged torso armour at its tier and which players farm here to prepare for the deeper bosses.

The Hydra's pool connects, through some subterranean route nobody has mapped, to the Moryskah swamp. Occasionally, something from the swamp comes up through the pool. The Hydra kills these things and does not eat them. What the Hydra eats is not clear.
bosses.kill_cry: Three heads. Three last breaths. They are out of sync.

bosses.name: The Veilmother
bosses.bestiary:
The Veilmother is the oldest Veil Tree at the centre of the sacred grove. She was sleeping. She is waking. The druids have spent a year trying to put her back to sleep and have failed because they were the ones who woke her, and they did not mean to, and the corruption that began when the Elder Druid was corrupted by something he will not name has spread through her root system in ways that cannot be sutured.

She is not, strictly speaking, a tree. The tree is the form her attention takes when she is not using her attention for anything else. When she engages, the trunk splits, and the roots lift, and she becomes a moving structure four metres tall that fights with her lower roots as lashing whips and with her upper branches as hammers and with her bark, which is harder than stone, as plating. The fight takes place inside the sacred grove and the grove does not make room. Trees get in the way. Stones obstruct lines of sight. The ground is soft where she wants it soft.

She is weak to slash — a blade can cut through wood, if the wood is wood, and she is at least partially wood. She resists ranged, because arrows lodge in her bark and do not penetrate to the living heartwood. Fire works, but fire in the sacred grove is a tactical choice with political consequences that will become apparent the first time an elf sees the scorch marks.

She drops her heartwood, which is a fragment the druids consider sacred and which sells for a great deal anyway, and the Verdant Plate, a piece of armour grown from her living bark that will, with care, mend itself between battles. She also drops the Root Whip, a piece of her lower root system that continues to live after her defeat and that strikes with a reach no ordinary whip can match.

When she falls, the grove falls with her — not all of it, but a ring of her nearest daughters bow their upper branches as if acknowledging something, and they remain bowed until the player has left. The druids do not accompany players out of the grove after the Veilmother's defeat. They do not speak until the player is beyond the forest's edge. What they are doing during that silence is not the player's business.
bosses.kill_cry: A single long sigh from everything that had been listening, and then the grove settles into a kind of quiet that had not been there before.

bosses.name: Vorath, Warden of the Deep Vein
bosses.bestiary:
Vorath is a construct. Dwarven-built, gnomish-assisted, commissioned by the third Forgemaster to guard the lowest gate of the deep vein against the things that come up the shaft. Vorath has worked continuously for four centuries. Vorath was not, in the design documents, supposed to still be working; the design documents assumed maintenance cycles, replacement parts, and the occasional scrap-and-rebuild. The cycles were maintained for the first two centuries. The cycles stopped. Vorath kept working.

Vorath is shaped like a dwarf and twice the size. Armour plating over a clockwork frame. Two arms, each ending in a blunt hammer-face larger than a player's head. A head that is a slit visor over a glowing core. The core is the part that has changed. The design documents describe a small steady red. The current core pulses, and the pulses are not regular, and when Vorath is angry — which is the only setting it still has — the core is nearly white.

It fights like a siege engine. Slow swings. Heavy damage. The hammer-faces break stone. Vorath has a stamp attack that cracks the floor and throws players off balance for two or three seconds, and a spin that clears the area around it of anything standing. It does not range. It does not need to. Nothing comfortable stands at its range.

Its weakness is magic. The clockwork frame conducts. A well-placed air spell will stagger its joints; a fire spell will overheat the core temporarily; an ice spell will lock its hammer arms for long enough to reposition. Melee is possible but punishing; ranged is actively wasted.

On death, Vorath's core cools, and the core can be pried out with care. The core is not a drop table item — it is a conversation with the Forgemaster, who will either allow the player to keep the core (rare) or trade it for the Molten Maul and Vorath's Anvil Ring (standard). The Forgemaster almost always chooses the standard trade. The few players who have kept the core have not explained why.
bosses.kill_cry: The core dims to a quiet red. The gate behind Vorath stops humming for the first time in four hundred years.

bosses.name: The Soot King
bosses.bestiary:
The Soot King is older than the Sootworks. He was in the hollow when the dwarves arrived, and the first Forgemaster bargained with him, and the terms of the bargain were that the dwarves would keep the central forge burning continuously, and that in exchange the Soot King would sleep, and that the bargain would renew for as long as the forge did not go out, and that the bargain would expire when the forge failed — as forges eventually do — and that the expiration would be at the Soot King's pleasure, not the dwarves'.

The forge has not gone out. The bargain is still technically intact. The Soot King is stirring anyway, because six hundred years is the longest any bargain of this type has ever held, and because the Soot King is calculating, and because the Sealed Vault where he rests is reachable by a corridor that the clockwork sentries no longer patrol correctly, and because the dwarves stockpiling soot-iron is a provocation he is choosing to interpret generously.

When he is fought — which is only after the Forge Beneath the City quest, and only by a team of three to five, and only with significant preparation — the Soot King is enormous. He stands almost four metres tall. He is humanoid, roughly, in the sense that an anvil is humanoid if you squint: thick limbs, a broad body, a head with a crown welded directly to the skull. The crown is industrial gems set in iron, which is why the crown is called the Soot King Crown, and which is why players want it.

He fights in three phases. First, the approach: he does not move, and he breathes forge-fire at the team, and the team must close through the fire. Second, the engagement: he fights with a great iron bar that he uses like a broom, sweeping the entire arena in wide arcs. Third, the core: at low health he opens his chest — a compartment of his body, not a metaphor — to reveal a furnace, and the furnace must be extinguished with a prepared charge, because if it is not extinguished, he ignites, and the team dies.

He is weak to magic. The iron frame conducts; the furnace is temperature-sensitive; the crown focuses spells that would otherwise scatter. He resists ranged — the gaps in his plating are narrow, and the plating is thick. Melee is workable but risky; stand too close and the iron bar will catch you.

Defeat awards the Soot King Crown, which is a melee-prayer hybrid helm that has no peer in its slot, and access to the sealed dwarven weapon cache which contains a generation's worth of preserved soot-iron bars. The Forgemaster attends personally when the crown is claimed. He does not speak during the claim. He bows, once, and he leaves.
bosses.kill_cry: The forge at the centre of the Sootworks flickers, once, and the dwarves in the hall around it hold their breath until it steadies.

bosses.name: Count Malachar
bosses.bestiary:
The Count is a vampyre, and the vampyres in Aelgard are not the vampyres of Heartlands folk-stories, which are sad creatures who cannot cross running water. The vampyres of Aelgard are an aristocracy with a biology. They age slowly, feed reluctantly, and reason clearly, and they remember everything. Count Malachar has been remembering things since the Malachar writ was signed, and the writ was signed seven centuries ago, and most of what he remembers concerns the people who were alive then and whose descendants are alive now, and his interest in those descendants is best described as proprietary.

He lives in Castle Malachar, in the south of the Moryskah swamp, in a keep whose foundations do not sink. He receives invitations — he extends them, actually — and he has extended one, recently, to the player, by means of a dead vampyre noble found in the raided village south of the swamp, with the invitation rolled in his hand. The invitation is real. The dinner, should the player accept it, is also real. The Count is a gracious host. He is not a safe one.

In combat, he is patient. He is not slow. He is faster than his size suggests — size two, but with a reach of five tiles — and his attacks drain health from the target and feed it to him, which means that staying at range is not a tactic so much as an obligation. He opens with a mist, which shortens the player's view of the arena for a few seconds. He closes with his hands, not a weapon; his nails are long and black and hardened. He will, at low health, bite, and the bite is harder to survive than anything else he does.

He is vulnerable to silver. Any silver weapon, including the Silver Sickle sold at Apothecary Nira's in the village, does twenty percent more damage. He is also vulnerable to consecrated ground — a vial of soil from the border chapel, prepared in the quest, will briefly immobilise him if thrown at his feet. Slash is his weakness in general terms; ranged bounces off the cloak he wears over his shoulders, which is not a cloak but something flatter and more functional.

He drops the Sanguine Cape (a blood-red cape that pulses slightly), Malachar's Signet (a ring that drains life on strike), and the Bloodwood Staff (carved from a tree that feeds on blood). He does not drop his crown. He will, on his second encounter with a returning player, offer the player a seat at his table, and the offer should be declined.
bosses.kill_cry: He says, very quietly, the name of the village his house was founded to protect. The name is not on any modern map.

bosses.name: The Kraken of Saltbrine
bosses.bestiary:
The Kraken was, for most of its life, far from shore. It lived in the deep trench that runs the length of the Reach's outer coast, and the trench was deep enough that no Reach boat had the ballast to dive for it, and the Kraken had no interest in surfacing. This arrangement worked. Something changed. The oldest fishermen say the singing from the trench has been getting louder for forty years, and in the last year the singing has moved, and the Kraken has moved with it, and the Kraken is now under the harbour.

Under, not at. The fight takes place in a flooded cave below the dock, reached through a tunnel that the cooperatives do not advertise and that can be navigated only with a waterbreathing potion prepared in Moryskah. The cave is lit by a glow from the Kraken itself, which is bio-luminescent in a way the old records did not mention.

The Kraken is size five. Most of the Kraken is out of range at any given time; the player fights tentacles, four of them, which protrude from the central body and which must be severed before the body becomes vulnerable. Each tentacle has its own hit points. Each tentacle has its own attack, mostly a grabbing strike but occasionally a whip. The body, when exposed, casts water magic — compressed spouts that punch through shields and staff spells that drain air from the lungs.

Weakness is slash. Tentacles cut. The body itself is tougher and takes reduced damage from magic — unlike most creatures of its scale, the Kraken is magical in its own right, and it resists the energies it wields. Ranged is viable but slow. Slash, specifically with a blessed weapon, clears the fight fastest.

It drops a severed tentacle as a weapon, which is itself a top-tier slash sword; the Tidal Amulet, which grants a magic-damage bonus underwater; and the Abyssal Trident, a powered staff that casts water magic without consuming runes. The Kraken also drops raw shark in respectable quantities, which has kept Mara's stall supplied through the last season's market shortfall.
bosses.kill_cry: The water in the cave stops moving. The singing, which the fishermen have been hearing for a year, stops, and does not resume.

bosses.name: The Inkweald Muse
bosses.bestiary:
The Muse is not a single creature. The Muse is what the Inkweald produces when a sufficient number of dreamers are dreaming in the same general direction, and the last time this happened, a version of the Muse coalesced in the deep forest and has not dissipated. The Keepers monitor her the way a weather station monitors a pressure system: as a phenomenon that is real, continuous, and not exactly a thing.

She appears as a woman, or as close to a woman as the Inkweald will commit to. Three metres tall. Robes that move in a wind that is not present. A face that resembles, in each player who sees it, a face the player has known and not seen in a long time. The resemblance is not flattering. The Muse has no particular malice toward the player — she has no particular anything — but she is in the way, and she will respond to being approached with a cascade of illusions that cannot be distinguished from her actual attacks except by recognising the pattern of her timing.

The fight is a five-player puzzle. Four players must watch for the true attacks in four different directions; the fifth must watch the Muse's face, because her expression changes in the frame before her real strike, and the change is too subtle for a single observer to catch reliably. Rotation is expected. Mistakes are expensive. Recovery is possible if the team has brought a Keeper's amulet, which corrects one misidentification per use.

She is weak to ranged. Her illusions absorb magic — spells feed her — and melee passes through her body the way a hand passes through a projected image, which is exactly what she is half the time. Arrows land, and land cleanly, and draw her out of the illusion state long enough to be engaged properly.

She drops the Muse's Mask, a hood that lets the wearer perceive truth more clearly than comfort permits, and the Dreamweaver Staff, a magic weapon that folds small pieces of the environment into itself between casts. She does not always drop on defeat. Sometimes the defeated Muse simply ceases to be present, and the drops appear later at the boundary camp, brought in by a Keeper who does not remember picking them up.
bosses.kill_cry: No sound. Yara, at the boundary camp a day's walk away, stops writing mid-sentence.

bosses.name: The Hollow Choir Conductor
bosses.bestiary:
The Conductor is the leader of the Choir and is possibly not a separate entity from the Choir but is, for purposes of engagement, addressed as one. The Choir sings. The Conductor directs. The singing reshapes the dream forest in real time, and the reshaping is a weapon. Players who enter the Resonance Chamber encounter the Choir first — a mass of singers arrayed in tiered ranks — and the Conductor last, after the tiers have been thinned and the chamber has been cleared of enough sound to make the Conductor's own voice audible.

Eight players. Three phases. The phases are distinguished by what the Conductor's weakness is, and the weakness cycles: phase one is crush, phase two is magic, phase three is ranged. Players who prepared only one combat style will fail. Players who prepared three will find the fight manageable and the survival rate acceptable.

The first phase is a close-range encounter in which the Conductor wields a baton that crushes what it touches. Shatter the resonance with crush weapons — maces, warhammers, mauls. The second phase takes place at middle range; the Conductor retreats to a dais and sings in a register that disrupts physical matter, and spells are the only attacks that reach him. The third phase is at extreme range; the Conductor ascends, and the Choir begins a harmonic that compresses the air between himself and the players, and only ranged weapons can punch through the compression at a distance that keeps the team safe.

The Conductor drops the Choir Sigil (a neck-slot item that resonates with impossible harmonics and grants a bonus to all combat styles simultaneously), the Harmonic Blade (a sword whose frequency disrupts armour), and the Silence Bow (arrows that produce no sound until impact). The drops are not all dropped in a single kill. The Conductor drops one of the three per defeat, and players who want the full set must clear him three times, and most teams find after the second time that they do not, in the end, want the full set, because the third run is when the Inkweald begins to notice them.
bosses.kill_cry: Silence. Actual silence. For several seconds afterward, even players' own breathing sounds muted.

bosses.name: The Glass Tyrant
bosses.bestiary:
The Tyrant is older than any other single creature on Aelgard. It is made of living crystal. It does not eat, does not sleep, does not age in any way the Crystal Sages can measure, and has been in the arena at the centre of the Glass Desert for the entire span of their recorded history. The Tyrant does not attack travellers unless travellers attack it. The Tyrant is not hostile. The Tyrant is territorial and the territory is defended with a thoroughness that makes the territoriality academic.

It stands four tiles tall. Its body is layered crystal plates that shift colour with the angle of the sun. It fights with a combination of crystal-shard projectiles, refracted-light beams, and direct melee strikes with limbs that are hard enough to crack stone. Its combat pattern cycles through three phases, and the phases are not subtle: phase one is melee only, and the player must close the distance; phase two is ranged only, because the Tyrant lifts from the ground and circles the arena at a height that melee cannot reach; phase three is magic only, because the Tyrant sheathes itself in a crystal barrier that deflects physical weapons and that can only be penetrated by spellwork that disrupts the crystal lattice.

The phase shifts are telegraphed. A rising tone announces phase two. A low vibration in the arena floor announces phase three. A player who prepared all three combat styles — a magic staff, a ranged weapon with appropriate ammunition, and a crush melee weapon — will find the fight difficult but fair. A player who prepared only one will die in the second phase.

Magic is its weakness. Ranged is its resistance. Glass reflects arrows. Spells disrupt the lattice.

The Tyrant drops the Glass Crown, which is a living-crystal helmet that shifts colour with the wearer's mood and which grants the best all-round defensive stats of any helm in Aelgard, and the Prismatic Blade, a layered sword whose each swing refracts the light differently and which ranks among the best one-handed melee weapons in the game. The Tyrant does not always fall. Some players have fought it for an hour and reported no discernible damage. The Sages say this is because the Tyrant chooses when to fall, and chooses to fall only for players who were going to fall to it otherwise, and that the Tyrant's philosophy about combat is older than any player's philosophy about anything.
bosses.kill_cry: The arena's crystal walls resonate, once, like a struck bell, and go still.

bosses.name: Veldrak, the Last Dragon
bosses.bestiary:
Veldrak is the last dragon of Aelgard. There were others. Veldrak is alone now because the others are dead, and Veldrak is alone now because Veldrak is what killed several of the others, and Veldrak is sleeping because the Crystal Sages — eleven of them, always eleven — each carry a fragment of the binding that holds the sleep, and the fragments are in the Sages' bodies, and they die with the Sage and are re-carved into the successor, and this has worked for eleven centuries and is beginning to slip.

The Last Dragon quest chain is three parts, and the third part is the awakening, and the awakening is triggered by the player's choice. The player may attempt to keep Veldrak asleep, which is the Sages' preference, or the player may wake Veldrak, because the prophecy etched in the oldest crystal says that Veldrak must be fought, once, before a certain event it does not name, and the Sages have not decided whether they believe the prophecy. The player decides. The player does not get to un-decide.

If woken, Veldrak rises, and the Glass Desert becomes a battlefield. Veldrak is the size of a small castle. His scales are crystalline and refract sunlight into a weapon. His breath is liquid fire that cools to crystal on the stone where it lands. He fights in three phases.

Phase one is Crystal Breath. Veldrak stands, grounded, and exhales in long sweeping arcs. Pray Magic; the breath's damage reads as spell rather than fire. Avoid the crystallised ground, which will trap a running player.

Phase two is Shattered Wings. Veldrak lifts. He becomes aerial and unreachable by melee. The ground around the player fills with crystal bombardment from above. Only ranged weapons hit him. Keep moving.

Phase three is Enraged. Veldrak descends, grounded again, and fights with his wings as well as his jaws and claws. All three styles work. None of them work well. A Dragonsbane weapon — forged in the quest chain from Moryskah consecrated materials and Sootworks soot-iron — is the only weapon that reliably penetrates his hide at this stage.

He is weak to stab. His scales overlap; the underbelly is vulnerable; a long pointed weapon reaches.

He drops the Dragon Shard, a fragment of his crystallised heart that is the most valuable crafting material in Aelgard; Veldrak's Talon, a sword that has no rival in its slot; and Veldrak's Scale Mail, a chestplate whose weight is negligible and whose defences are absolute against dragonfire. He also drops, always, five full dragon bones. The bones do not look like the bones of other dragons. They are longer and paler. The Sages collect them quietly.
bosses.kill_cry: A long exhale. The sky over the Glass Desert, which had been fire-red for the duration of the fight, cools to the white it was before.

bosses.name: The Revenant King
bosses.bestiary:
The Revenant King is the subject of the Wilds' deepest rumour and is, therefore, the Wilds' most valuable target. A revenant in a crown, in a crypt, in a ruin that is not on any surviving map of the old garrison. He is said to be what is left of the regent who led the Kingsfall expedition, though this is not confirmed. He is said to wear a crown that was made during the expedition, from a circlet the regent brought and from the teeth of the first revenant the regent killed, and this is also not confirmed. What is confirmed is that players who reach his chamber describe the same room, and the same figure, and the same crown, and the descriptions have been consistent across the small handful of reports spanning twenty years.

To reach him, a player must complete the Coronation quest, which requires finding the crypt — the crypt's location does not stay the same between expeditions and must be re-located on foot — and opening a door that the last few travellers to reach it declined to open. Opening the door is the quest. What comes after is the boss.

He fights as a spectral warrior. He moves silently. His strikes drain life and transfer it to him, and he heals faster than a single player can damage him. The fight is intended for a group of three or more; a solo player can win, but will need to have prepared extensively. He does not have phases in the conventional sense; he has moods, and his mood changes when his health drops below certain thresholds, and his attacks shift accordingly. He is faster at low health. His strikes are heavier when he is angry. He is angry most of the time.

He is weak to crush. The spectral form has no material skeleton but has a residual structure, and the structure shatters under blunt-force weapons the way a frozen thing shatters under a hammer. Slash passes through. Ranged lands but does reduced damage. Magic is variable.

He drops the Wilderness Crown, which grants a twenty percent damage bonus inside the Wilds and which does nothing at all outside them, and the Revenant Ether Mace, which is vampiric inside the Wilds and an ordinary mace outside. He also drops a quantity of gold and a map — hand-drawn, in his own script — of a part of the Wilds that is not on any existing crown map. The map has not been deciphered.
bosses.kill_cry: A long hollow breath. The crown, settled on his head a moment before, falls to the floor with the weight of something heavier than gold.

bosses.name: Osmumten, Pharaoh of the Desert
bosses.bestiary:
Osmumten is the raid boss at the heart of the Tombs of Aelgard, a pyramid in the deeper Wastes that was rediscovered after Azhmari's defeat loosened the sand over its entrance. He was a pharaoh earlier than Azhmari, and a more careful pharaoh, and his tomb was built for privacy rather than resurrection. He never expected to be disturbed. He also never expected to have stopped dying, which is the state he is currently in, and which he has expressed annoyance about through his attendants.

The tomb is an eight-player raid. Four pathways lead to four sub-bosses — the Warden of the Flame, the Warden of the Flood, the Warden of the Sands, the Warden of the Stars — and each Warden falls, and at the centre Osmumten rises from his sarcophagus and fights the party directly. He is tall, thin, and crowned. He wears no armour. He carries a fang — a curved blade of his own making, named Osmumten's Fang — and he wields it at close range with a precision that no other boss in Aelgard matches.

The Fang finds gaps in armour. Against high-defence targets, the Fang's accuracy doubles, and this is a passive property of the weapon that the pharaoh himself demonstrates in combat. His strikes always land. He does not miss. What a player can do is reduce the damage of a landing strike, and this is done through prayer, and the prayer cycle he requires is complex — he changes attack styles on a fixed tempo, and the tempo can be memorised, but the memorisation takes several runs.

The raid uses an invocation system. At base difficulty, the fight is merely hard. At maximum invocation — six hundred points' worth — the fight is the most difficult single encounter in Aelgard, and the rewards are proportional.

Osmumten drops his Fang (BIS stab against high-defence targets), Masori armour (a three-piece ranged set that maximises DPS at the cost of defence), the Lightbearer ring (halving special-attack restore time), Elidinis' Ward (the best magic shield available), and the Shadow of Tumeken (the most damaging magic weapon in Aelgard, powered by soul and chaos runes).
bosses.kill_cry: He lowers his fang slowly, inspects it, and speaks a single word to no one in particular. The word is his own name.

prestige_goals.name: The Grand Feast
prestige_goals.description:
In the Heartlands, you are not an adult in the old sense until you have sat at the Grand Hall table and survived its cooking. This is not a metaphor. The Grand Hall was the court kitchen once, and the Culinaromancers who ran it served meals that were courses of experience rather than courses of food, and the tradition of the Grand Feast is the survival of that older office: a three-course fight against a presence that is partly the Evil Chef, partly the kitchen, and partly the weight of a hundred meals served and a hundred diners remembered.

To own the Culinaromancer Gloves that mark the survivor is to say, without saying so, that the Heartlands recognises you. The crown does not issue this recognition; the Grand Hall does, and the Grand Hall does not consult anyone about its choices. The gloves are fingerless, soft leather, and they smell faintly of something pleasant that nobody can place. They are not valuable to sell. They are worth what they say about the wearer.

A player wearing the gloves in the Heartlands is greeted as a citizen. A player wearing them outside the Heartlands is treated as someone the Heartlands vouches for. Neither reaction is formal. Both are consistent.
prestige_goals.requirements_prose: The candidate must have proven themselves in the six Heartlands guilds — smiths, fishers, cooks, miners, warriors, magi — to the degree of holding a medallion. The candidate must have cleared the Grand Hall kitchen of the infestation that has occupied it since the last Culinaromancer vanished. The candidate must eat at the Chef's table one course at a time, surviving each, and in the end must decline the dessert the Chef offers, because the dessert is what the last Culinaromancer accepted.
prestige_goals.equivalent_to: A regional Quest Cape of sorts — the signal that a player has mastered the Heartlands' curriculum — but carried in leather gloves rather than a cape, and with a taste rather than a colour as its identifying mark.

prestige_goals.name: The Covenant's Seal
prestige_goals.description:
The elves do not award titles. The elves witness them. A player who has completed every quest in Veilwood, who has passed every ranged trial the Wardens have devised, and who has been accepted into the sacred grove on a solstice night — not by request but by invitation — is a player who has earned, in elvish terms, the Covenant's Seal. The Seal is not an item. It is a mark, barely visible, placed by a druid on the back of the left wrist with a thorn that leaves no scar.

An outsider with the Seal is not an elf. That is not what the Seal does. The Seal marks an outsider whom the forest will permit to move freely. It opens the doors of the sacred grove on any day rather than only solstices. It signals to the druidic circle that questions may be asked and may be answered.

To sell the Seal is impossible — it cannot be transferred. To fake the Seal is detected instantly; the elves see it the way a reader sees handwriting. Wearing it in the wrong place is the only risk: the Moryskah vampyres recognise it, and they are uncomfortable with elvish sanction, and discomfort in a Malachar is never a passive emotion.
prestige_goals.requirements_prose: Complete The Veilwood Covenant. Earn the rank of Warden by passing three ranged trials under the forest's scrutiny. Retrieve the heartwood of a fallen Veil Tree from the deep grove and return it to the Veilmother's bier. Witness the solstice ritual from inside the sacred grove without speaking. Be chosen by a druid to bear the thorn.
prestige_goals.equivalent_to: A regional mastery marker recognised by elves and resented by certain other factions, carried invisibly rather than worn.

prestige_goals.name: The Clockwork Heart
prestige_goals.description:
Dwarves build Clockwork Hearts because they believe that what a craftsman has built is a truer identity than what a craftsman was born into, and that building the right thing — once, specifically, with intent — proves the craftsman entitled to speak for the work. The Clockwork Heart is a mechanism the size of a fist, constructed from soot-iron plates, clockwork gears, a steam valve, and a single prism lens acquired from the Glass Desert. It ticks. It warms when held. It is built by the dwarves, one at a time, for candidates they deem ready.

A candidate does not commission a Clockwork Heart. A candidate earns the invitation to receive one. The invitation is extended by the Forgemaster's Council in private, after the candidate has completed Sootworks Rising, The Forge Beneath the City, and a handful of smaller tasks that the council does not advertise as part of the requirement — because they are tasks the candidate should do without being asked, and being asked would invalidate the test. The council notices.

To wear a Clockwork Heart is to be, in dwarven terms, a friend of the forge. It grants access to the deep vein's lower shafts — areas normally locked to outsiders. It grants the ability to commission custom soot-iron weapons at a meaningful discount. It signals, to every dwarf who sees it, that the wearer has been vouched for by the Forgemaster personally, and that mistreating the wearer is a mistake the council will redress.
prestige_goals.requirements_prose: Complete the three core Sootworks quests. Help a dwarf with a task that was not in a quest log. Carry a broken mechanism to Engineer Fizz and repair it personally. Forge a bar of soot-iron under the Forgemaster's supervision, without assistance, to his satisfaction. Decline the first offer of payment for any of these services. Accept the second.
prestige_goals.equivalent_to: A regional mastery marker worn on a chain around the neck, in full view, acknowledged publicly by the dwarves and dismissed as a curiosity by anyone else.

prestige_goals.name: The Salt King's Compact
prestige_goals.description:
There is no Salt King. That is the joke the nomads make when a traveller who has survived the Wastes asks what title they carry now. There is no Salt King, and the nomads laugh politely, and then they hand the traveller a small flask of oasis water, and the flask does not look valuable but it is, because the flask has been touched by the Hermit and marked with a sigil nobody outside the Wastes can read, and the sigil is the Compact.

The Compact is a bond, not an object. It is the Wastes' recognition of a traveller as a person who will not waste water, will not rob the dead without permission, will not fight the nomads' children, and will return in spring. In exchange, the nomads will guide the traveller through any sandstorm; the Hermit will answer questions; and the Bone Reef will part for the traveller at the third arch, showing a passage that the reef does not show otherwise.

The Compact is held by a small number of people and has never been held by more than two hundred of them at once. It is earned by completing every quest in the Wastes, by returning the Ancient Tablet to the nomads rather than to the Heartlands crown, and by declining to keep the treasure the Wastes provide. A traveller who keeps the treasure is not punished; the traveller simply does not receive the flask.
prestige_goals.requirements_prose: Complete Sand and Secrets and Relics of the Old World. Return the Ancient Tablet to Razak at the oasis rather than selling it to the Heartlands Museum. Bring three leviathan bones to the Hermit, one at a time, on three separate visits. Survive a sandstorm in the nomads' company. Promise, out loud, to return in spring. Return in spring.
prestige_goals.equivalent_to: A regional covenant carried as a small marked flask, almost unremarkable, whose meaning is understood only in the Wastes.

prestige_goals.name: Father Dorin's Ledger
prestige_goals.description:
Father Dorin keeps a book of the names of everyone who enters the Moryskah swamp, and he does not share it, and he does not have to, because Father Dorin is not a crown official and is not answerable to anyone but the dead whose names he is keeping. A player who has worked for Dorin for a long time — who has completed his quests, who has carried his letters, who has sat with him through a vigil — will eventually be offered a page in the book for their own name, and a page is the prestige.

The page is not the player's name. The page is the player's name plus, underneath, the names of everyone the player has brought safely out of the swamp. The count matters. Dorin does not pretend otherwise. A player with ten names under theirs is distinguished; a player with thirty is remembered; a player with a hundred, which has never happened, would be the first of a new category the book does not yet have a title for.

Owning a page means Dorin will speak to you without the formality he uses for everyone else. It means the border chapel is open to you at any hour. It means, in the swamp, that the vampyres recognise a protection Dorin extends, and the vampyres respect it, because they have had seven hundred years to test it and they have not found a way around it.
prestige_goals.requirements_prose: Complete The Bog Witch's Bargain. Complete Blood Rites. Carry three private letters from Father Dorin to recipients outside the swamp, and return with replies. Escort at least ten Moryskah travellers safely out of the swamp — the count is kept by the book, not by you. Sit a full vigil with Dorin on the night of the new moon.
prestige_goals.equivalent_to: A regional prestige measured not by item or title but by a name written on a specific page of a specific book, with other names appearing beneath it over time.

prestige_goals.name: The Tide-Reckoning
prestige_goals.description:
The fishing cooperatives hold an annual reckoning on the longest night of the winter, in which they read out the year's losses — boats taken, sailors drowned, pirates killed, prices collapsed — and in which they name the year's earners, in which they acknowledge each captain's contribution to the year's survival. The Tide-Reckoning is not a reward ceremony. It is a ledger event. But the cooperatives, in the course of the Reckoning, sometimes extend membership to an outsider who has earned it, and membership in the cooperatives is the Saltbrine prestige.

A member of the cooperatives is entitled to a share of the year's surplus. A member of the cooperatives is expected to attend the next year's Reckoning and contribute their own name. A member of the cooperatives may, if they choose, buy a share in a boat, or take a boat of their own, or simply draw the share and live at the Reach.

Membership is marked by a brass ring worn on the left ear. The ring is small. It is cast from a harbour anchor chain and it weighs almost nothing. It is recognised, on sight, by every port along the Aelgard coast and by several ports beyond.
prestige_goals.requirements_prose: Complete Pirate King. Complete Whispers from the Depths. Contribute at least one hundred lobsters to Mara's stall across the year. Decline a pirate's offer of employment within earshot of at least two cooperative captains. Attend the Reckoning on the longest night. Accept the ring when it is offered, and do not ask who nominated you.
prestige_goals.equivalent_to: A regional mastery marker worn as a small brass ring in the left ear, recognised across the Aelgard coast.

prestige_goals.name: The Lucid Initiation
prestige_goals.description:
The Lucid Keepers do not recruit. The Lucid Keepers accept. A candidate who has spent enough time at the boundary camp, and who has aided in enough Keeper tasks, and who has — crucially — not come apart under the Inkweald's attention, will eventually be offered the initiation. The initiation is a single night. The candidate sleeps at the camp, and dreams, and the dream is the interview.

The dream is not described, because nobody who has been through it agrees on what happened inside it. What is documented is this: the candidate wakes, and either the candidate is a Keeper or the candidate is not, and the Keepers know which, and the candidate knows which, and no outside observer knows which and no outside observer has ever been able to tell.

A Keeper is not required to wear anything or carry anything. A Keeper may travel freely and may take other work. What a Keeper is, functionally, is a person the Inkweald has agreed to leave alone, and this is worth more than any object, because the Inkweald is otherwise persistent. The Keeper may call on other Keepers for help. The Keeper receives, quietly, a small annual remittance from the order's vault.
prestige_goals.requirements_prose: Complete The Inkweald Door. Complete The Hollow Choir's Song. Spend three separate weeks at the boundary camp assisting Yara with routine Keeper tasks without payment. Record at least one paradox accurately in the camp's log. Sleep, when Yara offers the bed, and do not leave the dream before dawn.
prestige_goals.equivalent_to: A regional mastery signified by nothing visible and by being left alone by something that normally does not leave anyone alone.

prestige_goals.name: The Fang of Osmumten
prestige_goals.description:
In the deeper Wastes, beneath a tomb that Azhmari's defeat uncovered, Osmumten lies. He is a pharaoh older than the Sand Prince and better prepared for death, and his tomb was built to withstand the end of the world. A raid party of up to eight may enter, may navigate the four wardens, may face the pharaoh himself, and may return carrying his fang — a curved blade that belongs to him personally and that he wields against anyone who opens his tomb.

The Fang is the Tombs of Aelgard's signature drop, and owning a Fang is the Tombs' prestige. It is a stab weapon without peer against high-defence targets. Its accuracy against heavy armour is doubled; against thin armour, it is merely excellent. It cannot be sold cheaply, and is seldom seen outside serious raider circles, and is recognised instantly by anyone who has completed the raid even once.

To carry the Fang is to have been into the tomb and come out. This is not a small thing. The tomb has an invocation system — a way of scaling the raid's difficulty up to the limits of what a raid party can survive — and carrying a Fang at maximum invocation means a different thing than carrying a Fang at minimum. The distinction is carried on the Fang itself: a small engraving, updated on the weapon's hilt each time the raid is completed at a higher invocation level, is visible only to other Fang-bearers.
prestige_goals.requirements_prose: Complete Sand and Secrets. Complete Relics of the Old World. Enter the Tombs of Aelgard with a raid party. Defeat the four Wardens and Osmumten himself. Claim the Fang as your share of the drops. Ascend the invocation ladder to whatever level your party can bear.
prestige_goals.equivalent_to: A regional mastery carried as a weapon rather than a title, the Wastes' answer to the Fire Cape — a tool that proves its wielder by what it can do, not by what it is.

signature_items.name: The Cape of the Inner Fire
signature_items.description:
The Cape is not a trophy. The Cape is a consequence. Anyone who ascends the Fight Caves — sixty-three waves, alone, with the Crystal Sages' sanction and a small quantity of shark and prayer potions — receives the Cape as the reward. What the Cape is, in game terms, is a melee-oriented cape with strong all-round defensive stats. What the Cape is, in Aelgard terms, is proof that you did not give up.

It is red, and the red is not dyed. The Cape is woven from TzHaar thread, and the TzHaar thread is forged, not spun, and the forging is what gives the colour. The Cape cannot be sold. It cannot be traded. It can be worn, and it is worn, and every traveller who sees a Cape of the Inner Fire recognises the owner as a person who has ascended the Caves, because the Cape cannot appear on a person who has not. This is enforced at the metaphysical level; the Cape will unravel if worn by someone who did not earn it, and this has been tested.

A Cape-wearer is greeted differently in every region. In the Heartlands, a Cape-wearer is nodded to by the guard. In the Sootworks, a Cape-wearer is given a discount on certain forged goods. In the Wilds, a Cape-wearer is targeted first by PKers, because the Cape is red and visible and because the wearer is known to be tough, and the tough are preferred targets. In the Glass Desert, a Cape-wearer is left alone by the TzHaar, which is the most important recognition any wearer receives, and is not transferrable.
signature_items.origin: Woven by the TzHaar from their own forge-thread, delivered to any mortal who survives the sixty-three waves of the Fight Caves without fleeing, without help, and without lying. The Crystal Sages attest. The TzHaar deliver. The Cape is the only cape in Aelgard that has never been faked successfully.

signature_items.name: The Infernal Cape
signature_items.description:
The Infernal Cape is what comes after the Cape of the Inner Fire. Sixty-nine waves. A sealed descent beneath the Fight Caves, found rather than built, older than either the TzHaar or the Crystal Sages. The Infernal Cape is not red; it is deeper, closer to black at the centre and burning at the hem, and the heat from it is perceptible at arm's length even in cold weather.

In game terms, the Infernal Cape is the best cape in Aelgard for melee, ranged, and hybrid builds — a single item that no build can dismiss. In Aelgard terms, the Infernal Cape is proof. Not of what the wearer survived, though survival is implicit, but of what the wearer chose to attempt. The Infernal is voluntary. Few attempt it. Fewer complete it. The completion rate is public, and the number posted at the Glass Desert outpost is updated annually, and the number has been under one hundred for as long as the sign has existed.

To see an Infernal Cape on someone is to know that they have made, at some point, a decision nobody required them to make, and have survived it. Nothing else in Aelgard has this property. The Cape is silent about it. The wearer, usually, is too.
signature_items.origin: Awarded by no one to survivors of the Inferno. There is no ceremony. A traveller who emerges from the Inferno's final chamber will find the Cape already fastened around their shoulders. Nobody has witnessed the moment of fastening. Nobody who survives the Inferno can describe it.

signature_items.name: The Culinaromancer Gloves
signature_items.description:
Soft leather gloves, fingerless, dyed a faint cream colour that darkens slightly over years of wear. They are the finest melee gloves available in the early-to-middle game, and they do not advertise themselves. A traveller wearing them looks, from any distance, like a traveller wearing ordinary gloves. It is only on close inspection that the stitching becomes visible — the tiny wheat-and-flame sigil of the Grand Hall, worked in thread half a shade darker than the leather.

To wear them is to say, in the Heartlands, that you survived the Feast. The Heartlands does not make this explicit. The Heartlands never does. But a waiter at the Grand Hall tavern will, if asked, pour your drink without charging you. A guard at the north gate will nod. A grain crier in the market will tip his cap, once, and return to shouting prices.

The gloves smell faintly of something pleasant. It is not a food smell. It is not a soap smell. Former Culinaromancers, questioned by scholars, have each described the smell differently, and the scholars have concluded that the smell is the wearer's favourite thing to cook. This has not been proven. It is worth noting that the scholars find the conclusion embarrassing and publish it rarely.
signature_items.origin: Taken from the severed hand of the Evil Chef after the survival of the Grand Feast. The hand is Vessa's. The Lamplighters will, with consent, help bury it properly.

signature_items.name: The Sanguine Cape
signature_items.description:
Count Malachar wore the Sanguine Cape for two centuries. It is a blood-red cape that pulses, almost imperceptibly, with a slow beat that matches nobody's pulse and that does not match itself from day to day. The pulse is not alarming. It is almost soothing. Wearers report feeling calmer in combat than they otherwise would, and the report is consistent enough that the Lamplighters have begun a quiet study of the phenomenon.

In combat stats, the Cape is a high-tier prayer cape with strong all-round defensive coverage. What it offers in addition, and what is not in any published manual, is the ability of the wearer to resist the drain effect of other vampyres: a player wearing the Sanguine Cape does not lose life to a vampyre's touch the way other players do. This is not official. It is observed.

The Cape is traded, rarely, among the high-tier players. It is never given to someone the Count would have approved of. This is a rule the Moryskah vampyres enforce without discussing, and the enforcement is not violent, it is social: a Sanguine Cape worn in the presence of a vampyre noble who would have been friendly to the Count will cause the noble to leave the room and not return.
signature_items.origin: Dropped by Count Malachar when he falls, from his own shoulders, where he has worn it since long before any living witness. The Count does not always drop it; some kills reward the Signet or the Bloodwood Staff instead. Persistent players farm him over and over until the Cape comes.

signature_items.name: Malachar's Signet
signature_items.description:
A ring of black iron with a dark red stone, worn by Count Malachar on the third finger of his left hand for longer than any surviving document can trace. The stone is not a gemstone. It is something like a gemstone, and the Lamplighters refuse to look at it directly.

In combat terms, the Signet is a strong offensive ring — a bonus to all three melee strength styles, plus a smaller bonus to ranged and magic strength, plus a hitpoints requirement that ensures it cannot be worn by the unprepared. What the Signet does in addition, and what the Heartlands scholars have argued about for years, is that it drains life from whatever it strikes and redirects a small fraction of that life to the wearer. Not enough to compete with a dedicated lifesteal weapon. Enough to notice.

Wearing the Signet in Moryskah is read, by vampyres, as a kind of ironic statement. The Count's murderers wear his ring. It is recognised. It is not resented, quite — the vampyres are too old to resent anything petty — but it is observed, and the observation is filed.
signature_items.origin: Taken from Count Malachar's left hand after his defeat. The Count does not always drop it; the Cape and the Staff are alternatives, and the three-way drop rate means that a player who wants the Signet specifically must kill the Count multiple times.

signature_items.name: Veldrak's Talon
signature_items.description:
Veldrak's Talon is a single claw of the Last Dragon, fused at the haft into a grip that fits a mortal hand. It is not a crafted weapon — it is a trophy, honed. The blade's edge is the dragon's own, and the edge does not dull, because the edge is made of whatever Veldrak's body was made of, and that material does not wear in the way steel wears.

In game terms, the Talon is one of the best slash weapons in Aelgard — only the Prismatic Blade rivals it in its slot, and the Prismatic Blade has slightly lower base stats and a different tactical profile. The Talon strikes hard and fast and its hitting range is forgiving. It is also, to those who recognise it, a statement: the Talon cannot be faked, because the material is unique, and the material is unique because Veldrak is unique, and Veldrak is not available in quantity.

To wield the Talon is to say that you fought the Last Dragon and won. The Sages note each Talon that leaves the Glass Desert; they keep a list. The list is short. Not every Talon-bearer is remembered fondly by the Sages. The ones who woke Veldrak unnecessarily, in the Sages' estimation, are on the list with a small mark beside the name.
signature_items.origin: Taken from Veldrak's corpse in the final phase of the Last Dragon quest chain, by whoever lands the killing blow. The Sages observe. Veldrak does not drop the Talon every time; the Scale Mail and the Dragon Shard are alternative rare drops from the same fight.

signature_items.name: The Glass Crown
signature_items.description:
The Glass Crown is a crown of living crystal, taken from the head of the Glass Tyrant when the Tyrant falls. It shifts colour with the wearer's mood. The shifts are subtle; nobody has yet managed to read a wearer reliably from the colour, but several scholars have tried.

In combat terms, the Crown is the best all-round defensive helm in Aelgard: it covers stab, slash, crush, magic, and ranged defences at tiers higher than any comparable helm, and it adds magic and ranged offensive bonuses alongside a prayer bonus. It has no weak stat. This is rare for any piece of equipment and unprecedented for a helmet.

To wear the Glass Crown is to be read, at a glance, as a player who has engaged the Tyrant and was not diminished by the engagement. The Sages, who have a long memory and strong opinions, sometimes decline to speak to Crown-wearers they consider unworthy. Most wearers are considered worthy. The exceptions are publicised quietly among the Sages' listeners.
signature_items.origin: Dropped by the Glass Tyrant on the rare defeats the Tyrant allows. The Tyrant does not drop the Crown every time; the Prismatic Blade is an alternative tertiary drop. The Crown is never crafted. The Crown cannot be crafted. The material is not a material in the ordinary sense.

signature_items.name: The Soot King Crown
signature_items.description:
The Soot King's Crown is welded iron set with industrial gems — rubies, dark-blue sapphires, and a single black diamond in the centre. The crown is heavy. A mortal wearing it feels the weight the way a burden feels real on the shoulders. The weight is not merely physical. The gems, some Sootworks scholars have argued, have a psychological effect — the wearer stands straighter, speaks more deliberately, and is less likely to be interrupted.

In game terms, the Crown is a top-tier melee helm with prayer bonus and strength bonus — unusual for a helm, which usually chooses one or the other — and with strong defensive stats in all three melee categories. It is a melee player's helmet in a way no Glass Crown or Veldrak-scale helm manages to be. The Glass Crown is balanced. The Soot King Crown is partisan.

The Forgemaster attends each Crown-claim personally. He does not speak. He bows. The bow is not required by any ceremony. It is a private choice, and the dwarves have discussed it and have declined to codify it, because the Forgemaster's private choice is not a matter of council business.
signature_items.origin: Taken from the Soot King's head after his defeat in The Forge Beneath the City. The Crown does not always drop; the Soot-Iron Bar stockpile is the standard drop, and the Crown is tertiary, and multiple clearances may be required.

signature_items.name: The Verdant Plate
signature_items.description:
The Verdant Plate is armour grown, not forged. It is formed from the Veilmother's own bark after her defeat, cut into segments and worked by the druids into a chestplate fitted to the wearer. The plate is alive. It will, with care, mend itself between battles — small nicks close overnight, and larger damage heals over a matter of days, and the plate's maintenance is accordingly different from any metal armour.

In game terms, the Verdant Plate is a mid-to-high tier body armour with excellent melee defensive stats and a notable magic defence bonus, and a small prayer bonus. It is worn by druid-aligned players and by adventurers who want good stats without looking like a warrior. The armour is green-brown and its surface has the texture of polished wood.

The druids insist that the Veilmother's bark wants to return to the grove. Plate-wearers who die in distant regions have occasionally had their plates recovered and returned to Veilwood by agents nobody identified, and the plates have been placed by the Veilmother's bier, and they have remained there. The druids do not explain how this happens.
signature_items.origin: Harvested from the Veilmother's fallen form by the druidic circle, worked in silence for three days, and presented to whichever player struck the killing blow. The druids do not always present it; the Root Whip and the Heartwood are alternative drops, and the selection is not random — the druids decide.

signature_items.name: The Kraken Tentacle
signature_items.description:
The Kraken Tentacle is a severed limb, a sword-length piece of the Kraken's flesh that was cut off during the fight and that has not died since. It twitches when left alone. It is warm. It is used as a weapon — mounted on a short leather-wrapped haft and wielded as a high-end slash sword — and the wielding is uncomfortable at first and then habituating.

In game terms, the Tentacle is a slash weapon with strong melee stats and a small magic bonus, and it comes with a small vampiric property in underwater combat. Out of the water, the Tentacle is a slash weapon with strong melee stats. In the water, the Tentacle heals the wielder on successful strikes, and the healing is small but dependable.

The cooperatives at Saltbrine recognise the Tentacle instantly. A Tentacle-wielder is welcome at Mara's stall at any hour and is served without payment for small purchases. The larger purchases are paid as usual, because the cooperatives do not mistake hospitality for accounting.
signature_items.origin: Dropped by the Kraken when its central body is finally defeated, after the tentacles have been severed and the body exposed. The Tentacle is one of three possible drops — the Tidal Amulet and the Abyssal Trident are the alternatives — and farming the Kraken repeatedly is the method most players employ.

signature_items.name: The Tidal Amulet
signature_items.description:
The Tidal Amulet is a pendant on a kelp-rope, containing a drop of Kraken brine sealed in a small glass phial. The phial does not evaporate. The brine moves slightly when the wearer moves, as if responding to a tide the wearer cannot feel.

In game terms, the Amulet is a magic-focused neck slot with strong magic offensive bonuses, a small prayer bonus, and — distinctively — a magic damage bonus that scales larger in water or rain. It is the go-to amulet for water-aligned casters and for any caster fighting anywhere with moisture.

The cooperatives, again, recognise it. A Tidal Amulet is a signal. It is not as strong a signal as the Tentacle, because the Amulet is a caster's item and many casters do not frequent the Reach, but the recognition is there. The fishermen, particularly, will ask a Tidal Amulet wearer for a forecast — not for the weather, but for the deep sea, because the Amulet is believed to carry some of the Kraken's awareness, and the fishermen are willing to accept a guess.
signature_items.origin: Dropped by the Kraken of Saltbrine. One of three possible rare drops. The phial is sealed by a process nobody at the Reach has identified, and attempts to open the phial have all damaged the amulet without revealing the method.

signature_items.name: Azhmari's Crown
signature_items.description:
Azhmari's Crown is a golden diadem cut in the old Kherem style — long, narrow, banded with blue enamel, with a hawk's head at the front. It is the only pharaoh's crown in Aelgard currently outside a museum. It hums. The humming is not audible at a distance but becomes audible at arm's length, and the audible pitch is consistent, and the pitch is a note that does not belong to any known scale.

In game terms, the Crown is a magic-focused helm with prayer and magic bonuses and strong defensive stats in stab and crush. It is worn by magic-aligned players in the high mid-game. The hawk's head on the front catches light oddly; in full sun, it appears to look around.

The Hermit of the Old Sun, asked about the Crown, will answer — once — that the Crown is still receiving, and that whatever it is receiving is older than the Hermit's oldest memory. He will not say more. A Crown wearer who visits the Hermit is given water without payment. The other nomads treat the Crown as a danger rather than an honour; they will trade with a Crown-wearer, but they will not guide one.
signature_items.origin: Taken from Azhmari's head after his defeat in his throne room. The Crown is one of three possible rare drops — the Sandstorm Staff and the Bone Cleaver are the alternatives. Persistent Sand Prince killers collect all three over time.

signature_items.name: Osmumten's Fang
signature_items.description:
Osmumten's Fang is a curved blade, black-iron-dark, shaped like the tooth it is named after. It is short — shorter than most swords — and it is fast, and the point is the business end, and the business is puncturing armour. The Fang was the Pharaoh's personal weapon, and it was buried with him, and it came out with the party that defeated him.

In game terms, the Fang is a stab weapon with unusual properties. Against targets with high defence, the Fang's accuracy doubles — a passive effect encoded into the weapon itself. Against ordinary targets, it is a merely excellent weapon. It is the preferred weapon for any boss fight in which the opponent is heavily armoured, and the preferred weapon for several raid encounters, and a status item among serious raiders.

Fang-bearers can be identified by each other by a small engraving on the hilt, updated invisibly with each higher-invocation raid completed. The engraving is only visible to other Fang-bearers, and the invisibility is enforced by some property of the Fang itself, not by convention. Nobody has explained the mechanism.
signature_items.origin: Dropped by Osmumten at the climax of the Tombs of Aelgard raid. Loot depends on invocation level — higher invocation increases the drop rate. Multiple raids are typical before a party earns a Fang.

signature_items.name: The Wilderness Crown
signature_items.description:
The Wilderness Crown is a circlet of dark metal set with teeth — teeth from revenants, teeth from wolves, teeth from things harder to identify. It is worn by the Revenant King in his crypt, and it is taken by whoever defeats him. Inside the Wilds, the Crown grants a twenty percent damage bonus. Outside the Wilds, the Crown is a circlet of dark metal with teeth.

In game terms, this is the most context-dependent item in Aelgard. It is uncompetitive outside the Wilds and dominant within them. The bonus applies to all combat styles. A player wearing the Crown in the Wilds is a player to be avoided and then, when avoidance fails, to be engaged with full seriousness.

Crown-wearers are not subtle. The Crown is visible from a distance and the teeth catch light. Wearing it is a statement. The statement is: I was where you did not go, and I came back, and I came back with this. The Wilds rewards this kind of statement and punishes it. Crown-wearers die at a higher rate than non-Crown-wearers, because Crown-wearers are hunted first.
signature_items.origin: Taken from the Revenant King's head in the crypt, after completing the Coronation quest. The Crown does not always drop; the Revenant Ether Mace is an alternative, and the quest repeats imperfectly because the crypt is not in the same place twice.

signature_items.name: The Hydra Leather Body
signature_items.description:
The Hydra Leather Body is armour crafted from the scales of the Bog Hydra, tanned in the oasis water and stitched by one of the nomad tailors. It is a ranged torso armour — light, flexible, and built around protection against poison and corrosion. The scales are dark green, overlapping in rows, with a faint iridescence that catches light.

In game terms, the Hydra Leather Body is a strong mid-tier ranged armour with notable poison resistance. It is the standard choice for adventurers preparing to face poisonous creatures — bog hydras for training, sea snakes in Saltbrine, mummies in the Wastes, certain Moryskah monsters.

The armour smells, faintly, of the swamp. This does not fade. Wearers who spend time in the Heartlands report a persistent whiff of brackish water that follows them indoors, and some Heartlands innkeepers have asked Hydra-wearers to stable the armour overnight rather than bring it inside. The innkeepers are polite about it.
signature_items.origin: Crafted at Razak's camp from hydra scales acquired by defeating the Bog Hydra. The scales drop at a modest rate, and assembling a full body requires several defeats. The tailoring is the nomads' trade, and they charge a reasonable fee.

signature_items.name: The Silver Sickle
signature_items.description:
The Silver Sickle is a weapon made at Apothecary Nira's shop in Moryskah, out of silver she blessed herself under an older rite. It is not a masterwork. Its melee stats are modest — comparable to mithril-tier. Against vampyres, however, the Silver Sickle's damage increases by twenty percent, and this is the Sickle's entire reason for existing.

In game terms, the Sickle is a niche weapon. It is used exclusively in Moryskah and in the rare circumstance outside Moryskah where a vampyre appears elsewhere. Against non-vampyres, the Sickle is not competitive with tier-appropriate weapons. Against Count Malachar and his vampyre nobles, the Sickle is the single best weapon a player can bring.

Wearers of the Sickle — or carriers, since it is not usually worn in the sense of being always visible — are signalled as serious about the Moryskah problem. Father Dorin will nod to a Sickle-carrier. Grael the Bog Witch will speak to them at shorter distances. The vampyres will notice, and the notice is not friendly.
signature_items.origin: Purchased at Apothecary Nira's shop in Moryskah village, or — rarely — obtained as a quest reward from The Bog Witch's Bargain. The silver itself is mined in the Sootworks, traded to Nira through a chain of transactions that does not appear in any ledger, and blessed at the border chapel by Father Dorin.

signature_items.name: The Elven Bow
signature_items.description:
The Elven Bow is a composite bow of unusual craftsmanship, built by Fletcher Tarin from a single yew branch taken with permission from the sacred grove, strung with a bowstring of elven silk. It is light. It draws fast. It fires crystal arrows with a precision that no crown-made bow can match at its tier.

In game terms, the Bow is a high-tier ranged weapon — the standard choice for mid-game archers, and a long-lived favourite because its balance remains competitive at higher levels. It is one of Tarin's rare commissioned pieces; the off-the-shelf bow he sells at his shop is similar but not equivalent.

To carry the Elven Bow is to be recognised, by any elf, as someone who has passed the Covenant's ranged trial — because Tarin does not sell the bow otherwise. The trial is enforced. A player who somehow acquires the Bow without passing the trial will find that the elves are cool to them, and that the Bow's accuracy in the elves' presence is, mysteriously, lower than it ought to be.
signature_items.origin: Commissioned from Fletcher Tarin after passing the Covenant's ranged trial. The yew is taken from the sacred grove with druidic permission; the silk is spun by the elven weavers. The pricing is set by Tarin and has not changed in a generation.

signature_items.name: The Molten Maul
signature_items.description:
The Molten Maul is a two-handed crush weapon, forged at Vorath's own station and still retaining some of Vorath's heat. It glows, dimly, along its head. The glow does not fade. The Maul is heavy. A player below the minimum strength requirement cannot lift it cleanly. A player at the requirement can swing it, slowly, with force.

In game terms, the Maul is a strong crush weapon with exceptional strength bonuses and a slow attack speed. It is wielded by players who prefer to hit hard and infrequently, and it is particularly effective against armoured opponents — plate armour being the natural counter to crush.

The Maul's glow is warm but not burning. Wearers report that the grip stays comfortable even in long fights. The dwarves have studied the phenomenon and concluded that the residual heat is not thermal but sympathetic — the weapon remembers having been forged in the deep vein, and the memory is stable.
signature_items.origin: Dropped by Vorath on defeat. The Forgemaster's Anvil Ring is the alternative rare drop. Vorath must be defeated multiple times to collect both.

signature_items.name: The Dreamweaver Staff
signature_items.description:
The Dreamweaver Staff is a magic weapon taken from the Inkweald Muse after her defeat. It is a staff of pale wood, carved with sigils that do not hold still under close inspection, and its head is a small crystalline loop that does not refract the light it touches.

In game terms, the Staff is a high-tier magic weapon with strong magic offensive stats and an unusual passive: between casts, the Staff absorbs small pieces of the environment — a leaf, a pebble, a puff of dust — and folds them into itself, where they are never seen again. The absorptions do not affect the player's inventory. They affect only small, inconsequential details of the world around the player, and the details are not missed.

The Keepers request that Dreamweaver wielders not cast spells inside the boundary camp, because the Staff's passive interacts poorly with the barrier's mechanics. The request is polite. Most wielders comply.
signature_items.origin: Dropped by the Inkweald Muse. The Muse's Mask is the alternative rare drop. The Muse does not always drop on defeat — sometimes the defeated Muse simply ceases to be present, and the drops appear later at the boundary camp.

signature_items.name: The Muse's Mask
signature_items.description:
The Muse's Mask is a piece of headwear taken from the Inkweald Muse. It is a half-mask of pale ceramic, covering the upper face, with eye holes that are larger than they need to be. Wearing it is not uncomfortable. Looking through it is different from looking without it. The world, through the mask, is more transparent. The wearer sees illusions as illusions, traps as traps, and lies as lies. The wearer also sees, occasionally, things that were not meant to be seen, and this is the risk of the mask — the Inkweald does not love wearers who see too much.

In game terms, the Mask is a high-tier hybrid helm with magic and prayer bonuses and strong magic defence. It is favoured by hybrid players and by quest-focused adventurers who want reliable illusion detection.

The Keepers record Mask-wearers. They keep a list. The list is not shared. Mask-wearers are invited, once, to tea at the boundary camp, and the invitation is polite, and the tea is brief.
signature_items.origin: Dropped by the Inkweald Muse. One of two possible rare drops. The Mask's ceramic has been analysed by the Heartlands scholars and found to be a material for which no known kiln exists.

signature_items.name: The Choir Sigil
signature_items.description:
The Choir Sigil is a pendant taken from the Hollow Choir Conductor, composed of a thin silver disk inscribed with harmonic marks that shift slightly when not observed. The Sigil hums. The hum is below normal hearing. A wearer feels it more than hears it, as a slight vibration in the sternum.

In game terms, the Sigil is a neck-slot item that grants bonuses to all three combat styles simultaneously, plus a prayer bonus. It is the most flexible neck slot in Aelgard. Hybrid players wear it as default. Pure-style players wear it in any fight that has unclear prayer requirements.

The Sigil does not play well with other Hollow Choir items. Wearing the Sigil with the Harmonic Blade causes both to vibrate at frequencies that interfere with each other — not enough to damage the wielder, but enough to produce a low dissonance that Keepers find unsettling. The Silence Bow, worn alongside the Sigil, produces the opposite effect: the Bow's silencing and the Sigil's harmonic seem to balance. Pairs of Hollow Choir items are observed but not widely understood.
signature_items.origin: Dropped by the Hollow Choir Conductor at the end of the eight-player raid. The Sigil is one of three possible rare drops — the Harmonic Blade and the Silence Bow are the alternatives — and each kill yields one.

signature_items.name: The Bandos Chestplate
signature_items.description:
The Bandos Chestplate is taken from General Graardor, a deity-aligned boss in the God Wars Dungeon beneath the Wilds. It is heavy plate — a body armour with strong all-round defensive stats, a prayer bonus, and a small strength bonus that makes it the preferred body armour for melee players at its tier.

In game terms, Bandos gear is the workhorse high-tier melee set. It is not as flashy as Torva, not as specialised as Inquisitor's, but it is reliable, it is affordable at its tier, and it is what most serious melee players wear as default.

Bandos-wearers are not rare. The chestplate is common enough in the late-mid-game that its presence is not by itself a mark of prestige. What is a mark is a complete set — Bandos chest, Bandos tassets, Bandos boots, Bandos hilt combined with a Godsword blade — and complete-set wearers are noticeably wealthier and more prepared than the average late-mid-game adventurer. The full Bandos set signals commitment to melee as a primary style.
signature_items.origin: Dropped by General Graardor in the God Wars Dungeon. The dungeon is accessed through a deep entrance in the Wilds, and the Bandos stronghold is one of four deity halls. The drops are shared among party members after kills.

signature_items.name: The Masori Body
signature_items.description:
The Masori Body is a chestpiece built by the Masori order, an ancient group of ranged specialists whose headquarters lies beneath the Tombs of Aelgard. It is light cloth reinforced with feather-thin plates, colored deep indigo with gold threads. It is exceptionally flexible.

In game terms, the Masori Body is the BIS ranged DPS armour. Its ranged offensive and strength bonuses are the highest of any body armour. Its defensive stats, however, are lower than black dragonhide — the Body is a glass cannon. A full Masori set provides a damage bonus at the cost of incoming damage increase. Ranged players who live or die by DPS wear Masori. Ranged players who want to survive longer wear dragonhide.

The full set — Mask, Body, Chaps — is the raid-completion signal for ranged players. Bandos is the melee default; Masori is the ranged equivalent, and wearing the full set says that the player has completed the Tombs raid at invocation levels high enough to see the drops reliably.
signature_items.origin: Dropped inside the Tombs of Aelgard, scaling with invocation. One piece per raid is typical. Completing the set takes many runs.
